entries.title: 4624: An account was successfully logged on

detection.telemetry: Audit Logon (Success). Enabled by default on modern Windows.

fields.name: LogonType
fields.note: How the logon happened. 2=interactive, 3=network, 4=batch, 5=service, 7=unlock, 8=network cleartext, 9=new credentials (runas /netonly), 10=RemoteInteractive (RDP), 11=cached interactive.

fields.name: TargetUserName / TargetUserSid
fields.note: Account that logged on. Watch for SYSTEM noise and machine accounts ending in $.

fields.name: IpAddress / WorkstationName
fields.note: Source of the logon. Blank/'-' for local SYSTEM activity.

fields.name: LogonId
fields.note: Hex session id. Pivot to 4672, 4634/4647, and process 4688 events sharing this LogonId.

fields.name: LogonProcessName / AuthenticationPackageName
fields.note: Kerberos, NTLM, or Negotiate. NTLM to a domain-joined host can indicate lateral movement or misconfig.

entries.summary: Records every successful logon and, crucially, the LogonType that tells you whether it was someone at the keyboard, a network share, a service, or an RDP session.
entries.significance: The backbone of authentication triage. Type 10 (RDP), type 3 (network) from unusual hosts, and type 9 map to lateral movement and credential misuse. Correlate LogonId across 4624 -> 4672 -> 4688 to reconstruct a session.
triage: Read LogonType first, it changes the whole meaning of the event.
Check IpAddress/WorkstationName against expected sources for that account.
Pivot on LogonId to find privileges assigned (4672) and processes spawned (4688) in the same session.
For network logons (type 3), confirm the source host and account pairing is normal.
Flag NTLM (AuthenticationPackageName) where Kerberos is expected.

examples.label: RDP logons (type 10) in the last day
Sentinel, network logons by source IP
examples.code:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4624 and LogonType == 3
| summarize Count = count() by Account, IpAddress
| sort by Count desc

entries.caveats: Extremely high volume. SYSTEM (type 5) and machine-account (name ends in $) logons are normal background noise. Filter them out before hunting for human activity.

entries.title: 4625: An account failed to log on

detection.telemetry: Audit Logon (Failure). Enabled by default on modern Windows.

fields.name: SubStatus
fields.note: Why it failed. 0xC000006A=bad password, 0xC0000064=user does not exist, 0xC0000072=account disabled, 0xC0000234=account locked out, 0xC0000070=workstation restriction, 0xC000006F=outside logon hours.

fields.name: TargetUserName
fields.note: Account being attacked. Many failures for one user = guessing; one failure each across many users = spraying.

fields.name: IpAddress / WorkstationName
fields.note: Source of the attempt. A single external IP hitting many accounts is the classic spray signature.

fields.name: LogonType
fields.note: Type 3 (network) failures dominate remote attacks; type 10 = failed RDP.

entries.summary: A logon attempt was rejected. The SubStatus code is the key field, it distinguishes a fat-fingered password from a disabled account or a locked-out user.
entries.significance: The primary signal for brute force (T1110). Shape matters: many failures against one account is guessing (.001); a few failures across many accounts is password spraying (.003). Bursts of 0xC000006A from one source IP are the tell.
triage: Aggregate by TargetUserName and by IpAddress over a time window to see the attack shape.
Decode SubStatus, 0xC000006A (bad password) vs 0xC0000064 (user not found, i.e. enumeration).
Check whether any attacked account later shows a 4624 success from the same source (compromise).
Correlate with 4740 (lockout) to find accounts crossing the lockout threshold.

examples.label: Top attacked accounts and source IPs (last 24h)
examples.code:
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4625;StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-1)} |
  ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ User=$_.Properties[5].Value; Src=$_.Properties[19].Value } } |
  Group-Object User,Src | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count,Name -First 20

examples.label: Sentinel, password spray shape
examples.code:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize Failures = count(), Accounts = dcount(Account) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Accounts >= 10
| sort by Failures desc

entries.caveats: Service accounts with stale cached passwords, expired credentials on phones/mail clients, and scheduled tasks with old passwords all generate benign 4625 bursts. Baseline before alerting.

entries.title: 4634 / 4647: An account was logged off

detection.telemetry: Audit Logoff (Success). Default on.

fields.name: TargetLogonId
fields.note: Matches the LogonId from the paired 4624. Subtract times to get session duration.

fields.name: LogonType
fields.note: Same taxonomy as 4624; lets you scope logoffs to interactive vs network sessions.

entries.summary: Marks the end of a logon session. 4647 is a user-initiated logoff; 4634 is the session teardown. Pair with 4624 by LogonId to measure how long a session lasted.
entries.significance: Bounds a session's lifetime for timelining. Short-lived network sessions (type 3) that map to a burst of process creations can indicate remote command execution.
triage: Join to the originating 4624 on LogonId to compute session duration.
Use logoff time as the right edge when reconstructing what a session did.
Do not treat absence of a 4634 as suspicious, crashes and resets can drop it.
entries.caveats: Not perfectly reliable, abrupt shutdowns, RDP disconnects (see 4779), and resets may leave a session without a clean logoff.

entries.title: 4648: A logon was attempted using explicit credentials

detection.telemetry: Audit Logon (Success). Default on.

fields.name: SubjectUserName
fields.note: The already-logged-on account that supplied alternate credentials.

fields.name: TargetUserName / TargetServerName
fields.note: The account being used and the host it was aimed at. A mismatch between subject and target is the point of interest.

fields.name: ProcessName
fields.note: What launched the explicit-credential logon, runas.exe, a remote-admin tool, or a script.

entries.summary: Someone logged on with credentials different from their current session, runas, a scheduled task, or a tool connecting to a remote host with alternate creds.
entries.significance: A strong lateral-movement and credential-reuse signal. Attackers use explicit credentials to pivot; a normal user rarely does this. Subject != Target across many hosts is a pass-the-hash / credential-reuse pattern.
triage: Compare SubjectUserName to TargetUserName, differing accounts on an endpoint deserve a look.
Check ProcessName: unexpected tools supplying credentials are suspicious.
Fan out: does the same subject show 4648 to many TargetServerNames in a short window?
Correlate with 4624 type 3/9 on the target host.
entries.caveats: Legitimately generated by admins using runas, by scheduled tasks, and by some backup/management agents. Baseline your admin tooling.

entries.title: 4672: Special privileges assigned to new logon

detection.telemetry: Audit Special Logon (Success). Enabled by default.

fields.name: SubjectUserSid / SubjectUserName
fields.note: The account granted sensitive privileges. SYSTEM (S-1-5-18) fires this constantly and is noise.

fields.name: SubjectLogonId
fields.note: The link back to the 4624 for this session. This is how you turn 'a privileged logon happened' into 'who, from where'.

fields.name: PrivilegeList
fields.note: Which sensitive privileges were assigned, e.g. SeDebugPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege. SeDebugPrivilege is prized for LSASS access.

entries.summary: Fires when a logon is granted one or more sensitive/administrative privileges. It is logged at logon time, before the account has necessarily done anything.
entries.significance: The go-to marker for 'an admin-equivalent session started'. But SYSTEM triggers it constantly, so it is mostly noise on its own. Its value is correlation: match SubjectLogonId to the 4624 to learn who the privileged account is and where they came from.
triage: Filter out SYSTEM (SID S-1-5-18) and other service SIDs, that removes the bulk of the noise.
Take SubjectLogonId and join to the 4624 with the same LogonId to get the real user, source IP, and LogonType.
For remaining human accounts, confirm the privileged logon was expected on that host at that time.
Inspect PrivilegeList, SeDebugPrivilege / SeBackupPrivilege on a workstation is worth a second look.
Pivot to 4688 on the same LogonId to see what the privileged session executed.

examples.label: Non-SYSTEM privileged logons in the last day
Sentinel, privileged logons joined to source
examples.code:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4672 and SubjectUserName !in ('SYSTEM','LOCAL SERVICE','NETWORK SERVICE')
| project TimeGenerated, Account, SubjectLogonId
| join kind=inner (SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4624 | project SubjectLogonId=TargetLogonId, IpAddress, LogonType) on SubjectLogonId

entries.caveats: SYSTEM generates 4672 on essentially every boot and service start, this is entirely normal. Do not alert on raw 4672 volume; alert on privileged logons by human accounts on hosts where they should not appear.

entries.title: 4673 / 4674: A privileged service was called

detection.telemetry: Audit Sensitive Privilege Use. OFF by default and very noisy, enable tactically.

fields.name: PrivilegeList
fields.note: The privilege actually exercised, e.g. SeDebugPrivilege (open arbitrary process, used to read LSASS).

fields.name: ProcessName
fields.note: The process that used the privilege. mimikatz/procdump-like access to LSASS shows here.

entries.summary: Records the actual use of a sensitive privilege (4673) or an operation on a privileged object (4674), as opposed to 4672 which only records assignment.
entries.significance: SeDebugPrivilege use by an unexpected process is a credential-dumping tell. Because the category is so noisy it is usually off; when you do enable it, scope to specific privileges.
triage: Focus on SeDebugPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege usage by non-system binaries.
Correlate ProcessName with LSASS access (Sysmon 10) for credential theft.
Expect heavy volume, filter to a short list of privileges of interest.
entries.caveats: Off by default because normal software exercises privileges constantly. Enabling it broadly will bury you; enable only when hunting a specific technique.

entries.title: 4720: A user account was created

detection.telemetry: Audit User Account Management (Success). Default on.

fields.name: TargetUserName
fields.note: The newly created account. Odd names, or names mimicking service accounts, are suspicious.

fields.name: SubjectUserName
fields.note: Who created it. A new account created by a non-admin or off-hours is a red flag.

entries.summary: A new local or domain user account was created. On endpoints this is rare and high-signal; on domain controllers it is routine but still worth baselining.
entries.significance: Attackers create accounts for persistence (T1136). A 4720 followed quickly by 4728/4732 (adding the account to a privileged group) is a classic backdoor-account sequence.
triage: Confirm the account creation was expected and via the normal provisioning process.
Check who created it (SubjectUserName) and when, off-hours creation is suspicious.
Look for a fast follow-on 4728/4732/4756 adding the new account to Administrators or Domain Admins.
On workstations, treat any 4720 as noteworthy, local account creation is uncommon.
entries.caveats: Provisioning systems, MDM, and domain joins legitimately create accounts. Baseline your automation.

entries.title: 4722 / 4725 / 4726: Account enabled, disabled, or deleted

detection.telemetry: Audit User Account Management (Success). Default on.

fields.name: TargetUserName
fields.note: The account whose state changed.

fields.name: SubjectUserName
fields.note: The operator who made the change.

entries.summary: Lifecycle changes to an account: 4722 enabled, 4725 disabled, 4726 deleted. Re-enabling a dormant or previously disabled account is a common attacker move.
entries.significance: Attackers revive stale accounts (4722) to blend in, or delete accounts (4726) to cover tracks. A disabled service/admin account suddenly enabled and then logging on is a strong lead.
triage: For 4722, check whether the enabled account was dormant, then look for a subsequent 4624.
For 4726, confirm the deletion was an authorised offboarding action.
Tie the change back to the operator (SubjectUserName) and a change ticket.
entries.caveats: Routine HR offboarding and lab cleanup generate these. Context (which account, by whom, when) decides significance.

entries.title: 4728 / 4732 / 4756: Member added to a privileged group

detection.telemetry: Audit Security Group Management (Success). Default on. 4728=global group, 4732=local group, 4756=universal group.

fields.name: MemberName / MemberSid
fields.note: The account added to the group.

fields.name: TargetUserName
fields.note: The group name, Administrators, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins are the ones to watch.

fields.name: SubjectUserName
fields.note: Who performed the add.

entries.summary: An account was added to a security group. When the group is a privileged one (Administrators, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins), this is a direct privilege-escalation signal.
entries.significance: Adding a controlled account to Domain Admins is one of the highest-value escalation moves. A 4720 (new account) followed by 4732/4728 into a privileged group is a textbook backdoor.
triage: Alert on additions to Administrators, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins, Backup Operators.
Confirm the change matches an approved request; identify the operator (SubjectUserName).
Look back for a recent 4720 creating the added member.
Watch for quick add-then-remove pairs (4729/4733) used to hide temporary privilege use.
entries.caveats: Legitimate admin onboarding produces these. The privileged groups are few, alert tightly on those and baseline the rest.

entries.title: 4740: A user account was locked out

detection.telemetry: Audit User Account Management (Success). Default on. Logged on the authenticating DC / host.

fields.name: TargetUserName
fields.note: The locked account.

fields.name: CallerComputerName
fields.note: The source host that tripped the lockout, your first pivot to find the offending device.

entries.summary: An account crossed the failed-logon threshold and was locked. CallerComputerName points at the machine generating the failures.
entries.significance: Both a brute-force indicator and, at scale, a denial-of-service symptom. A wave of 4740s across many users points at a spray; repeated single-account lockouts often trace to a stale credential on a device.
triage: Pivot on CallerComputerName to find the source of the bad passwords.
Correlate with 4625 SubStatus 0xC000006A on the same source to confirm password guessing.
For single recurring lockouts, hunt for cached creds: mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mail clients, services.
For mass lockouts, treat as a spray / possible DoS and consider blocking the source.
entries.caveats: Very often benign, a user changed their password but a phone or mapped drive still uses the old one. Investigate source before assuming attack.

entries.title: 4768: A Kerberos TGT was requested (AS-REQ)

detection.telemetry: Audit Kerberos Authentication Service. Logged on domain controllers. Default on for DCs.

fields.name: TargetUserName
fields.note: Account requesting the ticket-granting ticket.

fields.name: IpAddress
fields.note: Source of the request.

fields.name: TicketEncryptionType
fields.note: 0x17 (RC4) where 0x12 (AES) is expected can indicate downgrade / older tooling.

fields.name: PreAuthType
fields.note: 0 (no pre-auth) flags accounts vulnerable to AS-REP roasting (T1558.004).

entries.summary: A domain account requested a Kerberos ticket-granting ticket, effectively the domain logon event, recorded on the DC.
entries.significance: The DC-side view of domain authentication. RC4 encryption where AES is expected, or PreAuthType 0, are the abuse signals (encryption downgrade, AS-REP roasting).
triage: Baseline TicketEncryptionType, sudden RC4 (0x17) for an account that normally uses AES is suspicious.
Flag PreAuthType 0 accounts (pre-auth disabled) as AS-REP roasting exposure.
Use IpAddress to map domain logons to source hosts.
entries.caveats: Extremely high volume on DCs. Legacy applications and some appliances legitimately use RC4. Baseline before alerting on encryption type.

entries.title: 4769: A Kerberos service ticket was requested (TGS-REQ)

detection.telemetry: Audit Kerberos Service Ticket Operations. Logged on domain controllers. Default on for DCs.

fields.name: ServiceName
fields.note: The SPN the ticket is for. A single account requesting tickets for many services is the Kerberoasting shape.

fields.name: TicketEncryptionType
fields.note: 0x17 (RC4) is the Kerberoasting favourite because the hash is offline-crackable. AES = 0x12/0x11.

fields.name: TargetUserName / IpAddress
fields.note: Requesting account and source host.

entries.summary: An account requested a service ticket for a specific SPN. This is the event that exposes Kerberoasting (T1558.003).
entries.significance: Kerberoasting requests RC4-encrypted service tickets in bulk to crack service-account passwords offline. The signature: one account, many distinct ServiceNames, TicketEncryptionType 0x17, in a short window.
triage: Hunt for one TargetUserName requesting many distinct ServiceNames quickly.
Filter TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4), the roasting encryption of choice.
Exclude machine accounts and known service brokers to cut noise.
Cross-check the requesting host and account against expected behaviour.

examples.label: Sentinel, Kerberoasting shape
examples.code:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4769 and TicketEncryptionType == '0x17'
| where ServiceName !endswith '$'
| summarize Services = dcount(ServiceName) by Account, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Services >= 10

entries.caveats: Legacy services still use RC4 legitimately. High baseline volume, always correlate distinct-SPN count per account rather than alerting on single tickets.

entries.title: 4771: Kerberos pre-authentication failed

detection.telemetry: Audit Kerberos Authentication Service (Failure). Logged on DCs.

fields.name: Status
fields.note: Failure code. 0x18 = bad password (the Kerberos equivalent of 4625 SubStatus 0xC000006A).

fields.name: TargetUserName / IpAddress
fields.note: Account and source of the failed attempt.

entries.summary: The DC-side record of a failed Kerberos authentication, the domain equivalent of a 4625 for password guessing against domain accounts.
entries.significance: Brute force and spraying against domain accounts surface here (Status 0x18). Aggregating by account and source reveals the same guessing/spraying shapes as 4625.
triage: Aggregate Status 0x18 by TargetUserName and IpAddress to see guessing vs spraying.
Correlate with 4740 lockouts and any subsequent 4768 success.
Baseline noisy sources (VPN concentrators, proxies) before alerting.
entries.caveats: Clock skew and expired passwords cause benign failures. High volume on DCs.

entries.title: 4776: NTLM credential validation

detection.telemetry: Audit Credential Validation. Logged where the account is validated (DC for domain accounts, locally for local accounts).

fields.name: Status / SubStatus
fields.note: 0x0 success; 0xC000006A bad password; 0xC0000064 no such user.

fields.name: LogonAccount
fields.note: The account being validated.

fields.name: SourceWorkstation
fields.note: The host that sent the NTLM request, your pivot for NTLM-based attacks.

entries.summary: Records NTLM authentication attempts (success and failure). The go-to event for tracking legacy NTLM auth and NTLM-based brute force.
entries.significance: NTLM where Kerberos is expected can indicate pass-the-hash, relay, or legacy misconfiguration. Failed 4776s aggregate into the same brute-force shapes as 4625/4771.
triage: Track NTLM usage by SourceWorkstation to find unexpected legacy auth.
Aggregate failures (0xC000006A) by account/source for brute force.
Investigate NTLM to sensitive servers where Kerberos should be used.
entries.caveats: Plenty of legitimate NTLM remains in most environments (older apps, IP-literal connections). Baseline before treating NTLM as malicious.

entries.title: 4688: A new process has been created

detection.telemetry: Audit Process Creation. Enable command-line capture via GPO: Administrative Templates > System > Audit Process Creation > Include command line. Not on by default.

fields.name: NewProcessName
fields.note: Full path of the launched executable. Binaries running from %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, or ProgramData are suspicious.

fields.name: CommandLine
fields.note: The full command line, only present if command-line auditing is enabled. This is where encoded PowerShell, LOLBins, and suspicious args show.

fields.name: ParentProcessName
fields.note: The spawning process. winword.exe or excel.exe spawning cmd/powershell is a classic macro-execution tell.

fields.name: TokenElevationType
fields.note: Whether the process ran elevated (%%1937 full token).

fields.name: SubjectUserName / SubjectLogonId
fields.note: Who ran it, pivot on LogonId back to the 4624/4672 session.

entries.summary: The single most useful execution event: what ran, from where, with what command line, and under which parent. Turn on command-line capture or you lose most of its value.
entries.significance: Process-tree reconstruction lives here. Office apps spawning shells, LOLBins (certutil, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32) with network args, and binaries in user-writable paths are all visible in NewProcessName + ParentProcessName + CommandLine.
triage: Enable command-line auditing first, without it CommandLine is blank and half the value is gone.
Build the parent/child tree: is the ParentProcessName a plausible launcher for the child?
Flag executables running from %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, ProgramData, or with random names.
Grep CommandLine for -enc/-EncodedCommand, DownloadString, mshta, regsvr32 /i:http, certutil -urlcache.
Pivot on SubjectLogonId to tie the process to a specific logon session and privilege level.

examples.label: Office apps spawning shells

entries.caveats: Very high volume. Management agents, patching, and login scripts create constant benign process activity. Baseline and hunt on parent/child anomalies rather than raw volume. Sysmon Event 1 is a richer alternative where deployed.

entries.title: PowerShell 4104: Script block logging

detection.telemetry: Enable Script Block Logging via GPO: Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging. Captures deobfuscated code.

fields.name: ScriptBlockText
fields.note: The actual script content PowerShell executed, deobfuscated. Encoded/compressed payloads are logged in their decoded form.

fields.name: MessageNumber / MessageTotal
fields.note: Large scripts split across multiple 4104 events; reassemble by Path/ScriptBlockId.

fields.name: Level
fields.note: Warning-level 4104 events flag content PowerShell's built-in heuristics consider suspicious.

entries.summary: Logs the full text of every script block PowerShell runs, after deobfuscation. This is the highest-fidelity view of what PowerShell actually did.
entries.significance: Defeats most PowerShell obfuscation because it logs the decoded block. -EncodedCommand payloads, Invoke-Expression chains, download cradles, and AMSI-bypass attempts are all readable here.
triage: Search ScriptBlockText for DownloadString, IEX, FromBase64String, -enc, Invoke-Mimikatz, AMSI bypass strings.
Reassemble multi-part blocks (MessageNumber/MessageTotal) before judging intent.
Prioritise Warning-level 4104 events, PowerShell already flagged them as suspicious.
Correlate to 4688/Sysmon 1 for the launching command line and parent process.

examples.label: Suspicious script blocks
examples.code:
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational' |
  Where-Object { $_.Id -eq 4104 -and $_.Message -match 'DownloadString|FromBase64String|IEX|Invoke-Expression|-enc' } |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Message -First 20

entries.caveats: Legitimate admin scripts, installers, and modules generate large volumes. Module logging (4103) and transcription complement this. Older PowerShell v2 can be used to evade v5 logging, hunt for 2.0 downgrade too.

entries.title: 7045: A new service was installed

detection.telemetry: Logged in the System log by the Service Control Manager. On by default. Security-log equivalent is 4697 (needs Audit Security System Extension).

fields.name: ServiceName
fields.note: Short, random, or single-character service names are a PsExec/remote-exec tell.

fields.name: ImagePath
fields.note: The binary or command the service runs. cmd.exe /c, powershell -enc, or a path in %TEMP%/ADMIN$ is highly suspicious.

fields.name: ServiceType / StartType
fields.note: Kernel driver services (type 1) can indicate a malicious/vulnerable driver (BYOVD).

entries.summary: The Service Control Manager installed a new service. This lands on both persistence (services survive reboot) and lateral movement (PsExec-style remote execution creates a temporary service).
entries.significance: PsExec and many C2 frameworks execute remotely by installing a transient service, a random ServiceName with an ImagePath pointing at cmd/powershell or a temp binary. Persistent malicious services also appear here first.
triage: Inspect ImagePath: cmd.exe /c, powershell -enc, rundll32, or a user-writable path is a strong lead.
Random/short ServiceName + short-lived service = PsExec-style remote execution.
Correlate with 4624 type 3 from the source host to confirm remote install.
For kernel-driver services, verify the driver's signature and reputation (BYOVD).

examples.label: Recently installed services
examples.code:
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System';Id=7045;StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-7)} |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, @{n='Service';e={$_.Properties[0].Value}}, @{n='ImagePath';e={$_.Properties[1].Value}}

entries.caveats: Software installs and driver updates legitimately create services. Baseline your deployment tooling; focus on ImagePath content and service lifetime rather than the raw event.

entries.title: 4697: A service was installed in the system (Security log)

detection.telemetry: Audit Security System Extension (Success). Not on by default, enable to capture service installs in the Security log alongside System-log 7045.

fields.name: ServiceName / ServiceFileName
fields.note: The service and the command it runs, same triage as 7045.

fields.name: ServiceType / ServiceStartType
fields.note: Auto-start and kernel-driver services warrant extra scrutiny.

entries.summary: The Security-log counterpart to System-log 7045. Useful when you centralise on the Security channel and want service installs in the same stream as logons.
entries.significance: Same detection value as 7045 (PsExec-style execution, service persistence) but in the audited Security log, which is often forwarded and retained more strictly.
triage: Treat identically to 7045: inspect ServiceFileName for shells, encoded commands, temp paths.
Enable Audit Security System Extension so this fires; otherwise rely on 7045.
De-duplicate against 7045 to avoid double-counting the same install.
entries.caveats: Off by default; if not enabled you will only see 7045 in the System log.

entries.title: 4698: A scheduled task was created

detection.telemetry: Audit Other Object Access Events (Success). Not on by default. Task Scheduler/Operational (106) also records task registration.

fields.name: TaskName
fields.note: The task path/name. Names mimicking legitimate tasks (e.g. under \Microsoft\Windows\) are used to blend in.

fields.name: TaskContent (XML)
fields.note: The full task definition. The Actions/Exec/Command and Triggers are where the payload and schedule live.

fields.name: SubjectUserName
fields.note: Who created the task.

entries.summary: A scheduled task was registered. Tasks are a top-tier persistence and execution mechanism (T1053.005), they survive reboot and can run as SYSTEM.
entries.significance: The task XML reveals the command, arguments, trigger, and run-as context. Tasks running powershell/cmd, pointing at temp paths, or triggering at logon/boot are classic persistence.
triage: Read the task XML Actions, what Command/Arguments does it run and as whom?
Check the Triggers, logon, boot, or short repetition intervals are persistence/beaconing tells.
Flag tasks placed under \Microsoft\Windows\ that are not Microsoft-signed work.
Correlate with 4688/Sysmon 1 when the task fires to see the resulting process.

examples.label: List non-Microsoft scheduled tasks
examples.code:
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskPath -notmatch '\\Microsoft\\' -and $_.State -ne 'Disabled' } |
  ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ Name=$_.TaskName; Path=$_.TaskPath; Action=($_.Actions.Execute -join ';') } }

entries.caveats: Software updaters, backup jobs, and management agents create many legitimate tasks. Baseline them and hunt on action content and trigger type.

entries.title: WMI-Activity 5857–5861: WMI operations and subscriptions

detection.telemetry: WMI-Activity/Operational log. On by default. 5861 records permanent event-consumer bindings (the persistence signal).

fields.name: 5861, ESS/consumer binding
fields.note: Records creation of a permanent __EventFilter to __EventConsumer binding, the WMI persistence primitive (T1546.003).

fields.name: 5857, provider load
fields.note: A WMI provider was loaded to host an operation; unusual providers can indicate abuse.

fields.name: 5858, operation errors
fields.note: Includes ClientMachine and query text; useful for tracing remote WMI activity.

entries.summary: The WMI-Activity/Operational log is the main native record of WMI abuse. Event 5861 in particular captures permanent event subscriptions used for stealthy persistence.
entries.significance: WMI event subscriptions (Filter + Consumer + Binding) run attacker code on triggers (e.g. at a certain time or on logon) with no file on disk in the usual autostart locations. 5861 is where that binding is recorded.
triage: Review 5861 for new CommandLineEventConsumer / ActiveScriptEventConsumer bindings.
Enumerate live subscriptions and compare to a known-good baseline (see the WMI persistence entry).
Trace remote WMI (5857/5858 ClientMachine) for lateral movement via wmic/Invoke-WmiMethod.
Correlate consumer command lines with 4688/Sysmon 1 execution.
entries.caveats: Legitimate management software (SCCM, monitoring) uses WMI subscriptions. Baseline existing consumers; alert on new or script-based ones.

entries.title: RDP 1149 / 21 / 25: Remote Desktop session events

detection.telemetry: Terminal Services operational logs. On by default. 1149=network auth succeeded (pre-logon), 21=session logon, 25=session reconnect.

fields.name: 1149, User / Source Network Address
fields.note: The account and source IP that passed RD Gateway/network authentication. Fires even before a full logon.

fields.name: 21 / 25, User / Source
fields.note: Successful session logon (21) and reconnect (25) with the session id and source address.

entries.summary: The dedicated RDP session logs. Together with Security 4624 type 10, they reconstruct who connected over RDP, from where, and when they reconnected.
entries.significance: RDP (T1021.001) is a favourite lateral-movement channel. 1149 gives you the source network address of the connector; 21/25 confirm the interactive session. External or unexpected source IPs are the alert.
triage: Correlate 1149 (source IP) with Security 4624 type 10 for the full picture of an RDP logon.
Flag RDP source addresses that are external or from non-admin subnets.
Use 25 (reconnect) to spot long-lived attacker sessions resumed over time.
Pivot to 4688 in the RDP session's LogonId to see what was run.
entries.caveats: Admins and jump hosts use RDP constantly. Baseline legitimate RDP source hosts and accounts; alert on new source/account pairings.

sources.label: Microsoft, Remote Desktop Services event logs

entries.title: 4778 / 4779: A session was reconnected / disconnected

detection.telemetry: Audit Other Logon/Logoff Events. Default on. 4778=reconnect, 4779=disconnect.

fields.name: AccountName / ClientAddress
fields.note: The account and the client address that reconnected or disconnected the session.

fields.name: SessionName
fields.note: The session identifier (e.g. RDP-Tcp#N).

entries.summary: Records reconnection (4778) and disconnection (4779) of interactive sessions, typically RDP. Disconnect-without-logoff leaves a session alive in the background.
entries.significance: Attackers often disconnect rather than log off, leaving tools running in a live session. Reconnects from new client addresses to an existing session are worth checking.
triage: Watch for 4779 (disconnect) without a following 4634/4647, the session is still active.
Flag 4778 reconnects from a different ClientAddress than the original connection.
Correlate with RDP 1149/21/25 and 4624 type 10.
entries.caveats: Normal in any RDP-heavy environment; users disconnect routinely. Use as corroboration, not a standalone alert.

entries.title: Run / RunOnce keys: autostart persistence

detection.telemetry: Not logged by default. Capture changes with Sysmon 13 (registry value set) or Security 4657 (Audit Registry). Snapshot with autoruns/reg query for hunting.

fields.name: Value name
fields.note: The arbitrary label for the autostart entry.

fields.name: Value data
fields.note: The command that runs at logon/boot. Paths in %TEMP%/%APPDATA%, rundll32, mshta, or powershell -enc are red flags.

entries.summary: The most common persistence location on Windows. Anything listed here runs automatically at user logon (HKCU) or system start (HKLM). RunOnce entries run once and delete themselves.
entries.significance: T1547.001. HKCU Run keys are writable by the user and need no admin rights, making them the default persistence for commodity malware. The value data is the payload command.
triage: List all Run/RunOnce values on the host and diff against a clean baseline.
Inspect value data for user-writable paths, LOLBins, and encoded commands.
HKCU entries persist per-user and survive without admin, check every profile, not just the current user.
Correlate the referenced binary with Prefetch/Amcache to confirm execution.

examples.label: Dump Run keys for all hives
examples.code:
'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run','HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run' |
  ForEach-Object { Get-ItemProperty -Path $_ -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue }

entries.caveats: Most Run-key entries are legitimate (updaters, sync clients, drivers). Baseline is essential, hunt on the value data and binary reputation, not the mere presence of entries.

sources.label: Microsoft, Run and RunOnce registry keys

entries.title: Winlogon Shell / Userinit: logon persistence

detection.telemetry: Not logged by default. Monitor with Sysmon 13 or Security 4657. Values should be exactly the Microsoft defaults.

fields.name: Shell
fields.note: Should be exactly 'explorer.exe'. Extra entries appended here launch at logon.

fields.name: Userinit
fields.note: Should be 'C:\Windows\system32\userinit.exe,'. Extra comma-separated paths run at logon.

entries.summary: Winlogon's Shell and Userinit values control what launches when a user logs on. Appending a payload (comma-separated) is a durable, high-privilege persistence technique.
entries.significance: T1547.004. Because the defaults are well known and rarely change, deviation is high-signal, any value beyond 'explorer.exe' / 'userinit.exe,' is suspicious.
triage: Compare Shell and Userinit to the exact Microsoft defaults; anything extra is suspect.
Examine appended paths for user-writable locations or scripts.
Check the Notify subkey (legacy) for DLL entries on older systems.
entries.caveats: Some enterprise login customisations legitimately modify Userinit. Confirm against your gold image.

entries.title: Services registry: service persistence & hijack

detection.telemetry: Service creation surfaces as 7045 / 4697. Registry edits captured by Sysmon 13 / Security 4657. Kernel drivers also live here.

fields.name: ImagePath
fields.note: The service binary/command. Points to the payload for a persistent service; watch for shells and temp paths.

fields.name: ServiceDll
fields.note: For svchost-hosted services, the DLL under Parameters. A hijacked ServiceDll runs inside a trusted svchost.

fields.name: Start
fields.note: 0/1 = boot/system-start driver, 2 = auto-start. Auto-start persistence survives reboot.

entries.summary: Services are defined entirely in the registry. Attackers create new services, hijack an existing service's ImagePath/ServiceDll, or set a FailureCommand to gain SYSTEM-level, reboot-surviving persistence.
entries.significance: T1543.003 / T1574. Services run as SYSTEM and start automatically, making them a powerful persistence and privilege position. svchost ServiceDll hijacks are especially stealthy.
triage: Pair registry findings with 7045/4697 to catch new services.
Diff ImagePath/ServiceDll values against baseline; flag temp paths and shells.
Check unquoted service paths with spaces (path-interception opportunity).
Verify driver services' binary signatures (BYOVD).
entries.caveats: Thousands of legitimate services exist. Focus on newly created services and value changes, not the full inventory.

entries.title: Image File Execution Options: debugger hijack

detection.telemetry: Not logged by default. Monitor with Sysmon 13 / Security 4657. A Debugger value on any binary is inherently suspicious.

fields.name: Debugger
fields.note: When set, the named program launches instead of the target exe. Set on sethc.exe/utilman.exe to get a SYSTEM shell from the login screen.

fields.name: GlobalFlag + SilentProcessExit
fields.note: The 'silent process exit' variant triggers a monitor process when the target exits, another execution/persistence path.

entries.summary: IFEO lets you attach a 'debugger' that launches in place of a target executable. Attackers point accessibility binaries (sethc.exe, utilman.exe) at cmd.exe for a pre-logon SYSTEM shell, or hijack other binaries for persistence.
entries.significance: T1546.008 / T1546.012. A Debugger value is almost never legitimate outside developer machines, so its presence is high-signal.
triage: Enumerate all IFEO subkeys with a Debugger value, treat each as suspicious.
Specifically check sethc.exe, utilman.exe, osk.exe, magnify.exe for a cmd.exe/powershell debugger.
Review SilentProcessExit MonitorProcess entries for the same abuse.
entries.caveats: GlobalFlag/tracing is occasionally used by developers and app-compat tooling. A Debugger pointing at a shell is not.

entries.title: WMI event subscription persistence

detection.telemetry: WMI-Activity/Operational 5861 records new bindings. Sysmon 19/20/21 record WMI filter, consumer, and binding activity, the best native coverage.

fields.name: __EventFilter
fields.note: The trigger, a WQL query (e.g. fire N seconds after boot, or on a process start).

fields.name: __EventConsumer
fields.note: The action, CommandLineEventConsumer runs a command; ActiveScriptEventConsumer runs VBScript/JScript.

fields.name: __FilterToConsumerBinding
fields.note: The link that activates the pair. All three must exist for the persistence to fire.

entries.summary: A fileless persistence technique: a WMI filter (trigger) is bound to a consumer (action) so attacker code runs on an event, with nothing in the usual Run/Startup locations.
entries.significance: T1546.003. Stealthy and often missed because it lives in the WMI repository, not on disk or in obvious autostart keys. Runs as SYSTEM.
triage: Enumerate __EventFilter, __EventConsumer, and __FilterToConsumerBinding in root\subscription.
Flag CommandLineEventConsumer / ActiveScriptEventConsumer that run scripts or shells.
Correlate with WMI-Activity 5861 and Sysmon 19/20/21 for creation time.
Baseline legitimate management subscriptions (SCCM, monitoring).

examples.label: List permanent WMI subscriptions
examples.code:
Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter
Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventConsumer
Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding

entries.caveats: Enterprise management tools legitimately register subscriptions. The technique is the binding of a script/command consumer to a trigger, baseline and alert on new ones.

entries.title: Persistence locations: where to look

detection.telemetry: No single log covers all of these. Combine Sysmon 13 (registry), 7045/4697 (services), 4698 (tasks), 5861/Sysmon 19-21 (WMI), and Autoruns snapshots.

fields.name: Rule of thumb
fields.note: There is no single persistence location, treat 'persistence' as a checklist across registry, services, tasks, startup folders, and WMI.

entries.summary: Persistence is not one answer, it is a set of autostart extensibility points (ASEPs). Junior analysts should learn the whole checklist rather than a single key.
entries.significance: When triaging a suspected foothold, sweep every autostart class: Run/RunOnce keys, Winlogon, services, scheduled tasks, startup folders, and WMI subscriptions. Sysinternals Autoruns enumerates most of them at once.
triage: Run Sysinternals Autoruns (or autorunsc for CLI) and hide Microsoft-signed entries.
Check each ASEP class listed above against a clean baseline.
For every autostart command, resolve the binary and check its path, signature, and execution artifacts.
Remember HKCU locations persist per-user and need no admin rights.
entries.caveats: Autoruns shows a large number of legitimate entries; the skill is filtering signed/known-good and focusing on the unusual.

entries.title: 1102: The audit log was cleared

detection.telemetry: Always logged in the Security log when it is cleared, cannot be disabled. One of the most reliable anti-forensics tripwires.

fields.name: SubjectUserName / SubjectUserSid
fields.note: The account that cleared the log. Legitimate clears are rare, attribute this carefully.

fields.name: SubjectLogonId
fields.note: Pivot back to the 4624 to learn where the clearing account logged on from.

entries.summary: The Security event log was cleared. Because Windows always logs this action (even as the log is wiped), 1102 is a near-guaranteed anti-forensics indicator.
entries.significance: T1070.001. Clearing the Security log is a deliberate, high-signal act, very few legitimate operations do it. Treat an unexplained 1102 as active adversary behaviour.
triage: Identify who cleared it (SubjectUserName) and pivot on SubjectLogonId to the source session.
Establish a legitimate reason, otherwise treat as adversary anti-forensics.
Check forwarded logs / SIEM: a good log pipeline retains events even after a local clear.
Look for the surrounding activity the clear was meant to hide (before/after the gap).

examples.label: Find log-clear events
examples.code:
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=1102} |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, @{n='ClearedBy';e={$_.Properties[1].Value}}

entries.caveats: Occasionally legitimate during maintenance or reimaging. The account, timing, and lack of a change record decide whether it is benign.

entries.title: 104: An event log was cleared (non-Security logs)

detection.telemetry: Logged when a non-Security log (System, Application, PowerShell, etc.) is cleared. On by default.

fields.name: SubjectUserName
fields.note: Who cleared the log.

fields.name: Channel
fields.note: Which log was cleared, clearing PowerShell/Operational or Sysmon logs hides execution evidence.

entries.summary: The 104 counterpart to 1102 for logs other than Security. Attackers clear System, PowerShell, and Sysmon logs to erase execution and service-install evidence.
entries.significance: T1070.001. Same anti-forensics weight as 1102 but for the logs that hold execution detail. Clearing the PowerShell/Operational or Sysmon logs is especially telling.
triage: Note which Channel was cleared, it tells you what the attacker wanted to hide.
Attribute via SubjectUserName and correlate to a session.
Rely on forwarded copies to recover the cleared content.
entries.caveats: Some maintenance scripts clear Application/System logs. Context decides; clearing Sysmon/PowerShell logs rarely has an innocent explanation.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK, Clear Windows Event Logs

entries.title: 4719: System audit policy was changed

detection.telemetry: Audit Audit Policy Change. Default on and cannot be practically disabled without itself logging.

fields.name: SubcategoryGuid / Subcategory
fields.note: Which audit subcategory changed. Disabling Logon, Process Creation, or Object Access auditing is a defense-evasion move.

fields.name: AuditPolicyChanges
fields.note: Whether success/failure auditing was added or removed.

fields.name: SubjectUserName
fields.note: Who changed the policy.

entries.summary: The audit policy was modified. Attackers disable specific auditing subcategories to go dark before acting, and the disable itself is logged here.
entries.significance: T1562.002. A 4719 that removes auditing from a sensitive subcategory, followed by a gap in those events, is a strong evasion sequence.
triage: Check which subcategory changed and whether auditing was turned off.
Correlate a disable with a subsequent absence of the expected events.
Attribute via SubjectUserName and confirm against change control.
Watch for auditpol.exe /clear or /set in 4688 command lines.
entries.caveats: Legitimate GPO refreshes and hardening projects change audit policy. Baseline expected changes; alert on ad-hoc local ones.

entries.title: 4657: A registry value was modified

detection.telemetry: Audit Registry (Success). OFF by default and requires a SACL on the specific key. Scope to autostart and security keys only.

fields.name: ObjectName
fields.note: The registry key path modified. Scope your SACLs to Run keys, Winlogon, Services, and Defender keys.

fields.name: OldValue / NewValue
fields.note: Before and after data, directly shows a persistence entry or a security setting being flipped.

fields.name: ProcessName / SubjectUserName
fields.note: What made the change and under whose account.

entries.summary: A native way to watch specific registry keys change without Sysmon. Because it needs a SACL and is noisy, you enable it only on high-value keys.
entries.significance: With SACLs on autostart and Defender keys, 4657 catches persistence installs and security-tampering (e.g. disabling Defender) in the audited Security log. NewValue shows exactly what changed.
triage: Deploy SACLs on Run/RunOnce, Winlogon, Services, and Defender policy keys.
Alert on NewValue writes to those keys and resolve the writing process.
Prefer Sysmon 13 where deployed, it is lower-friction than SACL-based auditing.
entries.caveats: Off by default and requires per-key SACLs; enabling broadly is extremely noisy. Most teams use Sysmon 13 instead.

entries.title: Defender 5001 / 5007 / 1116 / 1117: Microsoft Defender events

detection.telemetry: Defender operational log. On where Defender is the AV. 5001=real-time protection disabled, 5007=configuration changed, 1116=malware detected, 1117=action taken.

fields.note: Real-time protection was disabled, a common pre-attack evasion step.
A Defender setting changed; the value path shows what (e.g. exclusions added, tamper settings).
A threat was detected (1116) and an action taken (1117), the detection itself and its remediation.

entries.summary: The Defender operational events that reveal both real detections (1116/1117) and tampering (5001 disable, 5007 config/exclusion changes).
entries.significance: T1562.001. Attackers disable real-time protection (5001) or add path/process exclusions (5007) before dropping tools. A 1116 detection also tells you something already tried to run.
triage: Alert on 5001 (real-time protection off) and 5007 changes that add exclusions.
Treat new Defender exclusions as suspicious, a favourite way to whitelist a payload directory.
Use 1116/1117 to find what was detected and whether it was fully remediated.
Correlate disable events with subsequent execution (4688/Sysmon 1).
entries.caveats: Some legitimate software and admins add exclusions or toggle protection for performance. Baseline sanctioned exclusions; alert on unexpected changes.

entries.title: Sysmon 1: Process creation

detection.telemetry: Requires Sysmon installed with a config that logs ProcessCreate. Richer than Security 4688, includes hashes, parent, and OriginalFileName.

fields.name: Image / CommandLine
fields.note: The executable and full command line, always populated (unlike 4688 which needs command-line auditing on).

fields.name: Hashes
fields.note: MD5/SHA256/IMPHASH of the image, pivot to threat intel and find renamed binaries.

fields.name: ParentImage / ParentCommandLine
fields.note: Full parent context, the process tree with both command lines.

fields.name: OriginalFileName
fields.note: The PE's internal name, catches renamed LOLBins (e.g. a copy of powershell.exe renamed to update.exe).

entries.summary: Sysmon's process-creation event, the richest native execution telemetry available, with hashes, full parent/child command lines, and the binary's original filename.
entries.significance: The workhorse of endpoint hunting. OriginalFileName defeats binary renaming; Hashes enable intel pivots; ParentCommandLine gives the full tree. Preferred over 4688 wherever Sysmon is deployed.
triage: Reconstruct the process tree via ParentImage/ParentCommandLine.
Compare Image filename to OriginalFileName to catch renamed LOLBins.
Pivot Hashes/IMPHASH to intel and to other hosts running the same binary.
Hunt the same suspicious command-line patterns as 4688 (encoded PS, LOLBins, temp paths).
entries.caveats: Coverage and noise depend entirely on the Sysmon config (e.g. SwiftOnSecurity / Olaf Hartong baselines). A permissive config buries you; a tuned one is excellent.

entries.title: Sysmon 3: Network connection

detection.telemetry: Requires Sysmon with network logging enabled. Often filtered to specific processes/ports to control volume.

fields.name: Image
fields.note: The process that made the connection. powershell/rundll32/regsvr32 making outbound connections is suspicious.

fields.name: DestinationIp / DestinationPort / DestinationHostname
fields.note: Where it connected. Rare destinations and non-standard ports are C2 leads.

fields.name: Initiated
fields.note: True for outbound. Ties a specific process to a specific destination.

entries.summary: Maps processes to their network connections. The key event for tying an outbound C2 connection back to the exact process that made it.
entries.significance: Links execution to network. LOLBins or office processes connecting outbound, connections to rare IPs, and regular-interval connections (beaconing) all surface here when combined with process context.
triage: Attribute suspicious destinations to a process via Image.
Flag interpreters/LOLBins (powershell, rundll32, mshta) initiating outbound connections.
Hunt for regular-interval connections to the same destination (beaconing).
Enrich DestinationIp with intel/geo and known-good baselines.
entries.caveats: Browsers and updaters generate enormous connection volume, most configs filter Sysmon 3 heavily. Focus on unusual process/destination pairs.

entries.title: Sysmon 10: Process access (LSASS)

detection.telemetry: Requires Sysmon config that logs ProcessAccess to lsass.exe. Usually scoped to lsass to control volume.

fields.name: TargetImage
fields.note: The process being opened. Scope to lsass.exe for credential-dumping detection.

fields.name: SourceImage
fields.note: The process doing the opening. Anything other than known security tools opening LSASS is suspicious.

fields.name: GrantedAccess
fields.note: The access mask requested. 0x1010/0x1410/0x1438 (VM read + query) are the classic LSASS-dumping masks.

fields.name: CallTrace
fields.note: The call stack, helps distinguish tool-based access from legitimate OS access.

entries.summary: Records one process opening a handle to another. Scoped to LSASS, it is the premier detection for credential dumping (T1003.001).
entries.significance: Mimikatz, procdump, and comsvcs.dll MiniDump all open LSASS with high access masks. A SourceImage that is not a sanctioned security tool requesting 0x1010/0x1410 on lsass.exe is a strong credential-theft signal.
triage: Filter TargetImage = lsass.exe and review SourceImage against an allow-list of security tools.
Flag GrantedAccess masks including PROCESS_VM_READ (0x0010) combined with query rights.
Check CallTrace for unsigned modules or known dumping DLLs (comsvcs.dll MiniDump).
Correlate with 4688/Sysmon 1 for the command line (e.g. rundll32 comsvcs.dll).
entries.caveats: Some EDR/AV and diagnostic tools legitimately open LSASS. Maintain an allow-list of expected SourceImages to cut false positives.

entries.title: Sysmon 11 / 12 / 13 / 14: File and registry events

detection.telemetry: Requires Sysmon config targeting the keys/paths of interest. 11=FileCreate, 12=RegistryKey add/delete, 13=RegistryValue set, 14=RegistryKey/Value rename.

fields.name: 13, TargetObject / Details
fields.note: The registry value path and its new data. Scope to Run keys, Winlogon, Services to catch persistence with the payload command in Details.

fields.name: 11, TargetFilename
fields.note: Files created, dropper output, startup-folder LNKs, staged tools. Includes the creating Image.

fields.name: 12/14, key create/rename
fields.note: Key creation and rename operations, useful for IFEO and service-key manipulation.

entries.summary: Sysmon's file- and registry-monitoring family. Event 13 (registry value set) is the low-friction way to watch autostart keys and catch persistence as it is written.
entries.significance: T1547.001 / T1112. With a config scoped to autostart and security keys, Sysmon 13 records the exact value written to a Run key or Winlogon, payload command and all, without the SACL overhead of Security 4657.
triage: Scope Sysmon 13 to Run/RunOnce, Winlogon, Services, IFEO, and Defender keys.
Read Details for the written command and resolve the referenced binary.
Use Sysmon 11 to catch startup-folder LNK/file drops and staged tooling.
Correlate the writing Image with process-creation events.
entries.caveats: A broad config produces heavy registry/file noise. Target specific keys/paths; do not log all of HKLM.

entries.title: Sysmon 22: DNS query

detection.telemetry: Requires Sysmon 10+ with DNS logging enabled. Maps the querying process to the domain name.

fields.name: QueryName
fields.note: The domain queried. Long random subdomains suggest DNS tunneling; known-bad domains are direct hits.

fields.name: Image
fields.note: The process that made the query, attributing DNS to a non-browser process is valuable.

fields.name: QueryResults
fields.note: Resolved addresses, for enrichment and pivoting.

entries.summary: Attributes DNS lookups to the process that made them, filling the gap where network logs show the resolver but not the originating process.
entries.significance: C2 and DNS tunneling surface here: interpreters/LOLBins resolving unusual domains, long random-looking QueryNames, and beacon-like query cadence.
triage: Attribute suspicious domains to a process via Image.
Flag high-entropy / long subdomain QueryNames (tunneling).
Baseline normal domains per process; alert on interpreters resolving rare domains.
Correlate with Sysmon 3 for the subsequent connection.
entries.caveats: Very high volume; requires filtering. Browsers and updaters resolve countless domains legitimately.

entries.title: Sysmon 19 / 20 / 21: WMI event monitoring

detection.telemetry: Sysmon with WMI logging. 19=WmiFilter, 20=WmiConsumer, 21=WmiBinding. The clearest native view of WMI persistence creation.

fields.name: 19, EventFilter
fields.note: A new WMI event filter (trigger) was registered, with its WQL query.

fields.name: 20, Consumer
fields.note: A new consumer (action), CommandLineEventConsumer/ActiveScriptEventConsumer with the command/script.

fields.name: 21, Binding
fields.note: The filter-to-consumer binding that activates the persistence.

entries.summary: Sysmon's dedicated WMI-persistence events. Together, 19/20/21 capture the trigger, action, and binding of a permanent WMI event subscription as they are created.
entries.significance: T1546.003. These give creation-time visibility into fileless WMI persistence that the classic Run/Startup checks miss. Event 20 shows the actual command or script the consumer runs.
triage: Alert on Sysmon 20 consumers that run commands/scripts.
Reconstruct the full subscription from 19 (filter) + 20 (consumer) + 21 (binding).
Cross-check with WMI-Activity 5861 and live enumeration of root\subscription.
Baseline management-tool subscriptions; alert on new script-based ones.
entries.caveats: Legitimate management subscriptions exist; alert on new/unusual consumers rather than the presence of any subscription.

entries.title: Prefetch: evidence of execution

detection.telemetry: On by default on Windows client SKUs (often off on Servers). Collect with forensic imaging or a triage tool (KAPE); parse with PECmd.

fields.name: Executable name + hash
fields.note: Filename is NAME-HASH.pf; the hash is derived from the full path, so two paths to the same name produce different .pf files.

fields.name: Run count
fields.note: Number of times the program executed.

fields.name: Last run times
fields.note: Up to the last 8 execution timestamps, a mini timeline per binary.

fields.name: Referenced files/directories
fields.note: Files the program loaded, reveals payload paths and dependencies even after deletion.

entries.summary: Prefetch files prove a program executed, how many times, and when, even if the binary is now deleted. A cornerstone 'evidence of execution' artifact.
entries.significance: Confirms execution of tools that left no other trace. The referenced-files list can reveal payload locations; run counts and last-run times build a per-binary timeline. Absence of Prefetch for a known-run binary can itself indicate anti-forensics.
triage: Parse with PECmd (Eric Zimmerman) and sort by last-run time around the incident window.
Look for suspicious executables run from temp/user paths.
Use the referenced-files list to find payloads and loaded modules.
Note run count = 1 with a recent timestamp for one-off tool execution.
entries.caveats: Frequently disabled on servers and on SSD-tuned images. Only stores the last 8 run times (1024 entries max). Not a substitute for process logging, corroborate with 4688/Sysmon 1.

entries.title: Amcache.hve: execution & presence with hashes

detection.telemetry: Registry hive present by default. Parse with AmcacheParser (Eric Zimmerman). Records SHA1 for many entries.

fields.name: Full path + SHA1
fields.note: Path of the binary and, crucially, its SHA1 hash, enabling intel pivots even after deletion.

fields.name: Compilation / linker timestamps
fields.note: PE metadata that can flag recently-built or backdated binaries.

fields.name: First-seen time
fields.note: Approximate time the binary first appeared/ran on the host.

entries.summary: A registry hive tracking application presence and execution, and, unusually for a Windows artifact, the SHA1 of many recorded binaries.
entries.significance: The SHA1 hashes make Amcache excellent for threat-intel pivots and for identifying a deleted tool by hash. Combined with Shimcache and Prefetch it triangulates 'this binary was here and ran'.
triage: Parse with AmcacheParser and pull path + SHA1 for suspicious entries.
Pivot SHA1 to intel to identify known tooling.
Cross-reference with Shimcache and Prefetch to confirm execution vs mere presence.
Note that Amcache presence does not always guarantee execution, corroborate.
entries.caveats: Interpretation nuances have changed across Windows versions; presence in Amcache is strong evidence of the binary existing on disk but not always proof it executed. Use alongside Prefetch.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK, Application execution data source

entries.title: Shimcache (AppCompatCache): execution/presence order

detection.telemetry: Registry value written to disk at shutdown. Parse with AppCompatCacheParser. On by default.

fields.name: Path
fields.note: Full path of the executable that was present/run.

fields.name: Last modified time (of the file)
fields.note: The $StandardInfo last-modified time of the binary, not the execution time, a common misread.

fields.name: Insertion order
fields.note: Entries are ordered; relative order can help sequence activity.

entries.summary: The Application Compatibility Cache tracks executables the OS evaluated for shimming. A classic 'was this binary here' artifact, valuable because it survives deletion.
entries.significance: Records path and file-modified time for many executables, ordered by insertion. Useful for spotting tools that ran/were present and for approximate sequencing, especially on systems without Prefetch.
triage: Parse with AppCompatCacheParser and scan for temp/user-path executables.
Remember the timestamp is the file's modified time, not execution time.
The cache is written at shutdown, recent activity may not be on disk until the next reboot.
Corroborate with Amcache/Prefetch to distinguish presence from execution.
entries.caveats: Common misinterpretation: Shimcache does not by itself prove execution on modern Windows, and its timestamp is the binary's modified time. Treat as presence + ordering, corroborated by other artifacts.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK, Application execution data source

entries.title: SRUM: application & network resource usage

detection.telemetry: ESE database, on by default (Win8+). Parse with SrumECmd. Data flushed roughly hourly.

fields.name: Application + bytes sent/received
fields.note: Per-application network volume, invaluable for spotting exfiltration by an unexpected process.

fields.name: User SID
fields.note: Which user context drove the usage.

fields.name: Timestamp (hourly buckets)
fields.note: Coarse hourly aggregation of resource usage.

entries.summary: The System Resource Usage Monitor database records per-application network and resource usage over roughly 30–60 days, a rare native source of historical bytes-sent data.
entries.significance: Excellent for data-exfiltration triage: it can show a process that sent large volumes of data even when no packet capture exists. Ties application, user, and byte counts together historically.
triage: Parse SRUDB.dat with SrumECmd and sort by bytes sent per application.
Flag unexpected processes with large outbound volumes around the incident window.
Attribute usage to a user via the SID.
Treat timestamps as hourly buckets, not precise event times.
entries.caveats: Aggregated hourly and flushed periodically, not precise, and recent activity may not be committed yet. Best for volume trends, not exact timing.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK, Network traffic / exfiltration context

entries.title: LNK files & Jump Lists: file/opened-item history

detection.telemetry: Created automatically as users open files/apps. Parse with LECmd (LNK) and JLECmd (Jump Lists).

fields.name: Target path + volume info
fields.note: The full path of the opened file, including the original drive/volume, reveals access to removable media and network shares.

fields.name: Target MAC times
fields.note: Embedded created/modified/accessed timestamps of the target at the time of access.

fields.name: Jump List app id
fields.note: Ties recent items to the application that opened them.

entries.summary: LNK shortcuts and Jump Lists record which files a user opened, when, and from where, including files on USB drives and network shares that are no longer connected.
entries.significance: Proves a user accessed specific files and applications, and can reveal removable-media use and data staging. Timestamps and target paths survive after the file itself is gone.
triage: Parse Recent LNKs with LECmd and Jump Lists with JLECmd.
Look for access to sensitive files, staging directories, and removable/network volumes.
Use embedded target MAC times to place file access on the timeline.
Attribute activity to a user profile (artifacts are per-user).
entries.caveats: Reflects normal user activity too; the skill is spotting access relevant to the incident (staged archives, exfil sources, attacker tooling).

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK, File access data source

entries.title: UserAssist / BAM: GUI & background program execution

detection.telemetry: UserAssist logs GUI-launched programs (ROT13-encoded names); BAM/DAM records executables run per user with last-run times. On by default.

fields.name: UserAssist, program + run count + last run
fields.note: GUI-launched executables with focus time and run count. Names are ROT13-encoded.

fields.name: BAM, executable + last execution time
fields.note: Per-user last-run timestamp for background executables, a precise execution time source.

entries.summary: Two per-user execution artifacts: UserAssist tracks GUI-launched programs with run counts, and BAM/DAM records the last execution time of executables per user.
entries.significance: BAM gives a precise per-user last-run timestamp, often the cleanest answer to 'when did this user run this binary'. UserAssist confirms interactive (GUI) execution and frequency.
triage: Parse UserAssist (decode ROT13) for GUI-run tools and their run counts.
Use BAM last-run times to place a user's execution of a binary on the timeline.
Attribute to a specific user SID.
Corroborate with Prefetch/Amcache for the full execution picture.
entries.caveats: UserAssist only covers GUI launches (not scripted/CLI). BAM was reworked in later Windows builds, validate presence on the target version.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK, Application execution data source

entries.title: ShellBags: folder browsing history

detection.telemetry: Written as a user browses folders in Explorer. Parse with SBECmd. Per-user (UsrClass.dat).

fields.name: Folder path
fields.note: Folders the user opened in Explorer, including ones since deleted, on removable media, or on network shares.

fields.name: First/last interacted times
fields.note: When the folder was first and last viewed.

entries.summary: ShellBags record folders a user browsed in Explorer, including deleted, removable, and network locations, proving a user navigated to a path even after it is gone.
entries.significance: Demonstrates knowledge of and navigation to specific folders (staging areas, share paths, USB roots), which supports intent and data-access findings.
triage: Parse UsrClass.dat with SBECmd and review browsed paths.
Flag navigation to removable drives, network shares, and staging folders.
Use interaction times to sequence browsing on the timeline.
Combine with LNK/Jump Lists for file-level access.
entries.caveats: Records normal browsing too; relevance is context-dependent. Interpretation varies subtly by Windows version.

entries.title: Scheduled task files: on-disk task definitions

detection.location: C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ (XML per task) and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache
detection.telemetry: Each task exists as an XML file plus TaskCache registry entries. Compare on-disk XML to registry to spot hidden tasks.

fields.name: Task XML (Actions/Triggers)
fields.note: The command executed and its schedule, the payload and cadence of a persistence task.

fields.name: TaskCache\Tree + \Tasks
fields.note: Registry index of tasks. A task present on disk but manipulated in TaskCache can be hidden from the GUI.

entries.summary: The forensic, on-disk view of scheduled tasks. Pairing the Tasks XML files with the TaskCache registry catches tasks hidden from the normal UI.
entries.significance: Complements event 4698: even if the creation event is missing or cleared, the task's XML and TaskCache entries remain and reveal the command, trigger, and run-as context.
triage: Enumerate C:\Windows\System32\Tasks and read each XML's Actions/Triggers.
Diff on-disk tasks against TaskCache to find hidden/orphaned tasks.
Flag tasks running shells/encoded commands or triggering at logon/boot.
Correlate with 4698 and with execution at trigger time.
entries.caveats: Many legitimate tasks live here. Focus on non-Microsoft tasks and on action content, and on discrepancies between disk and registry.

entries.title: Startup folders: drop-a-file persistence

detection.telemetry: Anything (exe, script, LNK) placed here runs at logon. Monitor with Sysmon 11 (file create). No admin needed for the per-user folder.

fields.name: Dropped file / LNK
fields.note: The executable, script, or shortcut placed in the folder. LNKs pointing at scripts/temp binaries are the common pattern.

entries.summary: The simplest persistence: drop a file or shortcut into a Startup folder and it launches at logon, no registry edit or admin rights required for the per-user folder.
entries.significance: T1547.001. Low-sophistication but common. The all-users folder needs admin and affects everyone; the per-user folder needs nothing and affects that user.
triage: List both Startup folders and inspect every item, resolving LNK targets.
Flag shortcuts pointing at scripts, temp paths, or encoded commands.
Check every user profile, not just the active one.
Watch Sysmon 11 for new files created in these paths.
entries.caveats: Some legitimate apps add startup shortcuts. Resolve targets and check reputation rather than assuming malice.

sources.label: MITRE ATT&CK, Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder

entries.title: 4767: A user account was unlocked

detection.telemetry: Audit User Account Management (Success). Default on.

fields.name: TargetUserName
fields.note: The account unlocked.

fields.name: SubjectUserName
fields.note: Who unlocked it, helpdesk vs an unexpected operator.

entries.summary: An account that was locked out (see 4740) has been unlocked. Pairs with lockout events to show the response side of a brute-force incident.
entries.significance: Repeated lock/unlock cycles on the same account can indicate ongoing guessing plus manual intervention, or an attacker clearing their own lockout with stolen admin rights.
triage: Pair with 4740 to see lock/unlock cycles on an account.
Confirm the operator (SubjectUserName) is a legitimate helpdesk/admin.
Investigate the source of the failures that caused the original lockout.
entries.caveats: Routine helpdesk activity. Only interesting in the context of repeated lockouts or unusual operators.

entries.title: 1100: The event logging service was shut down

detection.telemetry: Logged when the Event Log service stops. Normal at shutdown; suspicious mid-session.

fields.name: TimeCreated
fields.note: When logging stopped. Compare to expected shutdown/reboot times.

entries.summary: The Windows Event Log service stopped. Expected during a clean shutdown, but a 1100 with no corresponding reboot can mean an attacker stopped logging to go dark.
entries.significance: T1562.002. A mid-session 1100 (no shutdown) is an evasion signal, often paired with a subsequent gap in events and, later, a 1102/104 clear.
triage: Correlate 1100 with actual shutdown/reboot events (6006/6008, System log).
A 1100 without a reboot is suspicious, look for the activity it was meant to hide.
Check for service stop commands in 4688/Sysmon 1 around the same time.
entries.caveats: Entirely normal at every clean shutdown. Only notable when it does not line up with a reboot.

entries.title: LSASS credential dumping: detection

detection.telemetry: Best coverage: Sysmon 10 scoped to lsass.exe, Sysmon 11 for .dmp creation, and command-line auditing on 4688. Defender/EDR also flags this.

fields.name: Access to lsass.exe
fields.note: Sysmon 10 SourceImage opening lsass.exe with masks like 0x1010/0x1410.

fields.name: Dump file creation
fields.note: Sysmon 11 creating lsass.dmp or similar in temp/user paths.

fields.name: Command line
fields.note: rundll32 comsvcs.dll MiniDump, procdump -ma lsass, or renamed variants in 4688/Sysmon 1.

entries.summary: Reading LSASS memory to extract credentials (T1003.001). Detect it via the process handle opened on lsass.exe, any dump file written, and the tell-tale command lines.
entries.significance: One of the highest-value attacker actions, it yields plaintext/hashes/tickets for privilege escalation and lateral movement. Multiple independent signals (handle, dump file, command line) make it detectable.
triage: Alert on Sysmon 10 access to lsass.exe from non-security-tool SourceImages.
Hunt Sysmon 11 for .dmp files, especially in temp/user paths.
Grep command lines for comsvcs.dll MiniDump, procdump -ma lsass, sekurlsa, nanodump.
Correlate with 4672/4673 SeDebugPrivilege use by the same process.
entries.caveats: EDR/AV and some diagnostics legitimately touch LSASS, maintain an allow-list. Attackers use LOLBins (comsvcs.dll) and renamed tools to evade name-based rules.

entries.title: T1110: Brute Force

detection.telemetry: Windows telemetry: 4625 (failed logon), 4771 (Kerberos pre-auth fail 0x18), 4776 (NTLM), 4740 (lockout). Aggregate by account and source over time.

fields.name: Sub-techniques
fields.note: T1110.001 Password Guessing, T1110.002 Password Cracking (offline), T1110.003 Password Spraying, T1110.004 Credential Stuffing.

fields.name: Attack shape
fields.note: Many failures/one account = guessing; few failures/many accounts = spraying; reused breach creds = stuffing.

entries.summary: Systematically guessing credentials. On Windows this is the story told by failed-logon telemetry, the shape of the failures tells you which sub-technique you are looking at.
entries.significance: The most common initial-access and escalation attempt against exposed authentication. Distinguishing guessing vs spraying vs stuffing drives the response (block source, reset account, enforce MFA).
triage: Aggregate 4625/4771/4776 failures by TargetUserName and by source IP over a window.
One account, many failures, one source = guessing (.001).
Many accounts, few failures each, one source = spraying (.003).
Check whether any targeted account then shows a success (4624) from the attacking source.
Correlate lockouts (4740) to find accounts crossing the threshold.

examples.label: Sentinel, spray vs guess in one view
examples.code:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize Failures=count(), Accounts=dcount(Account) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated,1h)
| extend Shape = iff(Accounts>=10,'spray', iff(Failures>=20,'guess','low'))
| where Shape != 'low'

entries.caveats: Benign sources abound: stale cached credentials, expired passwords on devices, and misconfigured services. Baseline before alerting; MFA success after failures may still be legitimate.

entries.title: T1110.001: Password Guessing

detection.telemetry: 4625 / 4771 concentrated on a single account from a source, often tripping 4740 lockouts.

fields.name: Signature
fields.note: Many failed logons against one account in a short window from one (or few) sources.

entries.summary: Guessing passwords for a specific known account against a live service, the noisiest brute-force variant, frequently triggering lockouts.
entries.significance: Targets a chosen account (often an admin or service account). Loud and lockout-prone, so usually easy to spot in 4625 aggregation.
triage: Aggregate 4625 by TargetUserName; a single account with a failure spike is the tell.
Identify and block/investigate the source.
Check for a subsequent 4624 success (compromise) and 4740 lockouts.
entries.caveats: A single misconfigured device repeatedly using an old password mimics guessing. Confirm the source is not a benign stale credential.

entries.title: T1110.003: Password Spraying

detection.telemetry: 4625 / 4771 spread thinly across many accounts from one source, few failures per account to dodge lockout thresholds.

fields.name: Signature
fields.note: One source, many distinct target accounts, low failures each (often 1–2), over a broad window.

entries.summary: Trying one or a few common passwords against many accounts to stay under lockout thresholds. Quieter than guessing and easy to miss without cross-account aggregation.
entries.significance: A leading cause of account compromise because it evades per-account lockout logic. Detection requires counting distinct accounts per source, not failures per account.
triage: Aggregate 4625 by source IP counting dcount(distinct accounts) per window.
A single source touching many accounts with low per-account failures is the spray signature.
Look for the one success hiding among the failures.
Enforce MFA and consider blocking the source.

examples.label: Sentinel, spray detection
examples.code:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize Accounts=dcount(Account) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated,1h)
| where Accounts >= 10

entries.caveats: VPNs, NAT, and shared egress IPs can make many benign users look like one source. Correlate with geography and known infrastructure.

entries.title: T1110.004: Credential Stuffing

detection.telemetry: 4625/4776 from external sources using known breach credentials; successes (4624) may follow immediately with no prior failures for that exact pair.

fields.name: Signature
fields.note: Login attempts using username/password pairs from prior breaches; high success-per-attempt versus spraying.

entries.summary: Replaying username/password pairs stolen from other breaches. Because the credentials are often correct, it can produce immediate successes with little failed-logon noise.
entries.significance: Dangerous precisely because it is quiet, valid reused passwords may authenticate on the first try. MFA is the primary control.
triage: Watch for successful external logons (4624 type 3) from unusual geographies without prior failures.
Cross-reference authenticating accounts against breach-exposure data.
Prioritise MFA enforcement and impossible-travel detections.
entries.caveats: Low failed-logon signal makes it hard to catch with 4625 alone, lean on successful-logon anomalies and MFA telemetry.

entries.title: T1078: Valid Accounts

detection.telemetry: No single event, hunt anomalies in 4624/4672/4648: unusual source, time, LogonType, or privilege for the account.

fields.name: Why it is hard
fields.note: Uses real credentials, so authentication succeeds cleanly. Detection is behavioural, not signature-based.

fields.name: Key signals
fields.note: Logon from a new host/geo, off-hours, unusual LogonType, or sudden privileged logon (4672).

entries.summary: Using legitimate credentials to blend in across initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, and evasion. The successful logons look normal, detection is about deviation from baseline.
entries.significance: Spans four ATT&CK tactics because valid accounts are the ultimate living-off-the-land tool. The whole point is that individual events look benign; anomalies emerge only against a behavioural baseline.
triage: Baseline each account's normal source hosts, times, and logon types.
Alert on deviations: new source/geo, off-hours, unexpected 4672 privileged logon.
Correlate 4648 explicit-credential use and lateral movement across hosts.
Tie suspicious sessions to what they did via LogonId -> 4688.
