entries.caveats: High false-positive potential, legitimate travel, new devices, and role changes look like anomalies. Tune with context and MFA signals.

entries.title: T1059: Command and Scripting Interpreter

detection.telemetry: 4688 with command-line auditing, Sysmon 1, and interpreter-specific logs (PowerShell 4104).

fields.name: Interpreters
fields.note: cmd, PowerShell (.001), Windows Script Host wscript/cscript (.005), and others.

entries.summary: Abusing built-in command and script interpreters to run code. The parent umbrella for PowerShell, cmd, and WSH execution on Windows.
entries.significance: Nearly every intrusion touches an interpreter. Parent/child anomalies (Office spawning a shell) and suspicious arguments are the detections.
triage: Reconstruct process trees from 4688/Sysmon 1.
Flag interpreters spawned by Office/browsers or running encoded commands.
Route PowerShell activity to the 4104 script-block view.
entries.caveats: Interpreters run constantly for legitimate admin and software tasks. Hunt on context, not presence.

entries.title: T1059.001: PowerShell

detection.telemetry: Script Block Logging (4104), Module Logging (4103), transcription, plus 4688/Sysmon 1 for the launching command line.

fields.name: Red flags
fields.note: -enc/-EncodedCommand, DownloadString/DownloadData cradles, IEX, FromBase64String, AMSI bypass, hidden/NoProfile.

entries.summary: Using PowerShell for download cradles, in-memory execution, and post-exploitation. The single most abused interpreter on Windows.
entries.significance: Powerful, native, and scriptable, ideal for living off the land. Script Block Logging (4104) is the key defence because it logs deobfuscated code.
triage: Search 4104 for cradles, encoded/compressed payloads, and AMSI-bypass strings.
Catch PowerShell v2 downgrade used to evade v5 logging.
Tie execution back to a parent process and user session.
entries.caveats: Admin automation is heavy PowerShell. Baseline sanctioned scripts and signing.

entries.title: T1027: Obfuscated Files or Information

detection.telemetry: PowerShell 4104 logs deobfuscated blocks; 4688/Sysmon 1 show -enc arguments and high-entropy command lines.

fields.name: Common forms
fields.note: Base64/-EncodedCommand, gzip+base64, string concatenation, and character-code obfuscation.

entries.summary: Hiding payloads and commands through encoding, packing, or obfuscation to defeat static detection.
entries.significance: Ubiquitous in scripts and droppers. Script Block Logging defeats most PowerShell obfuscation by logging the decoded content.
triage: Prefer 4104 (decoded) over raw command lines for PowerShell.
Flag -enc and long base64 blobs in command lines.
Decode and inspect payloads for the real intent.
entries.caveats: Some legitimate tooling encodes arguments. Decode before judging.

entries.title: T1053.005: Scheduled Task

detection.telemetry: 4698 (task created), Task Scheduler/Operational 106, and on-disk Tasks XML + TaskCache.

fields.name: Abuse
fields.note: Tasks run payloads at logon/boot/interval and can run as SYSTEM. Names may mimic Microsoft tasks.

entries.summary: Using Task Scheduler for persistence and execution, including SYSTEM-level and remotely-created tasks.
entries.significance: Durable, flexible, and often overlooked. The task XML reveals the command, trigger, and run-as context.
triage: Review new/non-Microsoft tasks' Actions and Triggers.
Flag tasks running shells/encoded commands or triggering at logon/boot.
Correlate 4698 with on-disk Tasks XML to catch hidden tasks.
entries.caveats: Many legitimate tasks exist; focus on action content and provenance.

entries.title: T1547.001: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 13 on Run keys, Security 4657 with SACLs, Sysmon 11 for startup-folder drops, and Autoruns snapshots.

fields.name: Locations
fields.note: HKLM/HKCU Run and RunOnce; per-user and all-users Startup folders.

entries.summary: The most common autostart persistence: registry Run keys and Startup-folder items that launch at logon or boot.
entries.significance: HKCU Run keys and the per-user Startup folder need no admin rights, making them commodity-malware favourites.
triage: Enumerate Run/RunOnce across HKLM and every HKCU hive.
Inspect Startup folders and resolve LNK targets.
Flag user-writable paths, LOLBins, and encoded commands.
entries.caveats: Full of legitimate entries, baseline and hunt on the value data.

entries.title: T1543.003: Windows Service

detection.telemetry: 7045 / 4697 (service installed), Services registry, Sysmon 13 for value changes.

fields.name: Abuse
fields.note: Create a new service, hijack ImagePath/ServiceDll, or set FailureCommand, all run as SYSTEM and start automatically.

entries.summary: Installing or hijacking a Windows service for SYSTEM-level, reboot-surviving persistence (and often execution).
entries.significance: Services run privileged and auto-start; svchost ServiceDll hijacks are stealthy. Also the mechanism behind PsExec-style execution.
triage: Catch new services via 7045/4697; inspect ImagePath/ServiceDll.
Flag shells, temp paths, and unsigned driver services (BYOVD).
Diff service registry against baseline.
entries.caveats: Thousands of legitimate services, focus on new/changed ones.

entries.title: T1569.002: Service Execution

detection.telemetry: 7045/4697 for the transient service, 4624 type 3 from the source, and 4688/Sysmon 1 for the spawned command.

fields.name: Signature
fields.note: A short-lived service with a random name and an ImagePath pointing at cmd/powershell or a temp binary.

entries.summary: Executing commands by installing and starting a (usually transient) Windows service, the mechanism behind PsExec and many C2 lateral-movement modules.
entries.significance: A primary lateral-movement pattern. The tell-tale is a random, short-lived service running a shell or temp binary, tied to a remote network logon.
triage: Correlate 7045 with 4624 type 3 from the source host.
Inspect ImagePath for shells/encoded commands/temp paths.
Follow the spawned process via 4688/Sysmon 1.
entries.caveats: Legitimate remote admin also uses services. Confirm the source and intent.

entries.title: T1021.001: Remote Desktop Protocol

detection.telemetry: 4624 type 10, RDP 1149/21/25, and 4778/4779 reconnect/disconnect.

fields.name: Signals
fields.note: RDP from unexpected source hosts/subnets, or between workstations that never normally connect.

entries.summary: Moving laterally via interactive RDP sessions using valid credentials.
entries.significance: A favourite hands-on-keyboard lateral-movement channel. Source-host anomalies are the detection.
triage: Join RDP 1149 (source IP) to 4624 type 10.
Flag external or workstation-to-workstation RDP.
Follow session activity via LogonId -> 4688.
entries.caveats: Admins and jump hosts use RDP constantly, baseline legitimate paths.

entries.title: T1021.002: SMB / Windows Admin Shares

detection.telemetry: 4624 type 3, 5140/5145 (file share access), and 7045 for service-based execution over the share.

fields.name: Signals
fields.note: Access to ADMIN$/C$/IPC$ from unusual sources, often preceding service-based remote execution.

entries.summary: Using SMB and the hidden administrative shares (ADMIN$, C$, IPC$) to move laterally and stage tools.
entries.significance: Underpins PsExec-style execution and tool staging. Network logons plus share access from an unusual source are the pattern.
triage: Watch 4624 type 3 with admin-share access (5140/5145) from unexpected hosts.
Correlate with 7045 service installs for remote execution.
Baseline legitimate admin and backup traffic.
entries.caveats: Backup and management tools use admin shares heavily. Baseline before alerting.

entries.title: T1546.003: WMI Event Subscription

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 19/20/21 (filter/consumer/binding) and WMI-Activity 5861; enumerate root\subscription.

fields.name: Primitive
fields.note: __EventFilter (trigger) + __EventConsumer (action) + __FilterToConsumerBinding, running as SYSTEM.

entries.summary: Fileless persistence via permanent WMI event subscriptions that run attacker code on a trigger.
entries.significance: Stealthy and often missed by classic autostart checks; runs privileged. Sysmon 19/20/21 give creation-time visibility.
triage: Alert on new script/command consumers (Sysmon 20).
Reconstruct filter+consumer+binding and enumerate root\subscription.
Baseline management-tool subscriptions.
entries.caveats: Legitimate management uses WMI subscriptions, alert on new/unusual ones.

entries.title: T1546.008: Accessibility Features

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 13 / 4657 on IFEO keys; file integrity on sethc.exe/utilman.exe; 4688 for cmd launched pre-logon.

fields.name: Method
fields.note: Replace or IFEO-debugger accessibility binaries (sethc, utilman) so the login screen launches a SYSTEM shell.

entries.summary: Abusing accessibility binaries to get a pre-authentication SYSTEM shell from the logon screen.
entries.significance: Grants SYSTEM without logging in. A Debugger value on an accessibility binary is almost never legitimate.
triage: Check IFEO Debugger values on sethc/utilman/osk/magnify.
Verify accessibility binaries are the genuine signed files.
Look for cmd/powershell launched at the logon screen.
entries.caveats: Rare legitimate developer use of IFEO tracing; a shell debugger is not legitimate.

entries.title: T1047: Windows Management Instrumentation

detection.telemetry: WMI-Activity/Operational 5857/5858, Sysmon 1 for wmic.exe/WmiPrvSE child processes, 4688.

fields.name: Abuse
fields.note: Win32_Process Create for local/remote execution; recon via WMI classes; subscriptions for persistence (.003).

entries.summary: Using WMI for execution, reconnaissance, and lateral movement, a native, low-footprint technique.
entries.significance: WMI is everywhere and trusted, so it blends in. WmiPrvSE.exe spawning shells is a key execution tell.
triage: Flag WmiPrvSE.exe spawning cmd/powershell (remote WMI exec).
Trace remote WMI via 5857/5858 ClientMachine.
Separate benign management WMI from ad-hoc use.
entries.caveats: Management platforms use WMI constantly, baseline heavily.

entries.title: T1112: Modify Registry

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 12/13/14, Security 4657 (with SACLs), and 4688 for reg.exe/PowerShell registry edits.

fields.name: Uses
fields.note: Persistence (Run keys), evasion (disable Defender/security settings), and hiding configuration/state.

entries.summary: Creating, modifying, or deleting registry data for persistence, evasion, or to store configuration.
entries.significance: The registry underpins persistence and many security settings. Scoped monitoring of sensitive keys catches both.
triage: Monitor autostart and Defender/security keys with Sysmon 13 or SACL-based 4657.
Resolve the writing process and read the new value.
Flag disabling of security settings.
entries.caveats: The registry changes constantly, scope to high-value keys.

entries.title: T1070.001: Clear Windows Event Logs

detection.telemetry: 1102 (Security cleared), 104 (other logs cleared), 1100 (service stopped), and 4688 for wevtutil/Clear-EventLog.

fields.name: Signals
fields.note: 1102/104 clears, or a suspicious 1100 with no reboot, followed by an event gap.

entries.summary: Clearing Windows event logs to remove evidence, a deliberate anti-forensics act that is itself logged.
entries.significance: Because the clear generates 1102/104, it is a reliable tripwire. Forwarded logs preserve the evidence the attacker tried to erase.
triage: Alert on any 1102 and on 104 for Security-adjacent logs.
Attribute via SubjectUserName and pivot to the source session.
Recover cleared content from the SIEM / forwarded logs.
entries.caveats: Rare legitimate clears during maintenance, context decides.

entries.title: T1562.001: Disable or Modify Tools

detection.telemetry: Defender 5001/5007, Sysmon 13/4657 on Defender policy keys, 4688 for Set-MpPreference / sc stop.

fields.name: Methods
fields.note: Turn off real-time protection, add path/process exclusions, stop AV/EDR services, or tamper with config.

entries.summary: Disabling or weakening security tooling, turning off Defender, adding exclusions, or killing agents, to clear the way for tools.
entries.significance: Frequently precedes payload execution. New Defender exclusions are a classic 'whitelist my payload directory' move.
triage: Alert on 5001 (RTP off) and 5007 exclusion changes.
Watch for Set-MpPreference and service stops on AV/EDR.
Correlate disable events with subsequent execution.
entries.caveats: Admins legitimately tune AV. Baseline sanctioned exclusions.

entries.title: T1562.002: Disable Windows Event Logging

detection.telemetry: 4719 (audit policy changed), 1100 (log service stopped), 4688 for auditpol/Set-Service, and event gaps.

fields.name: Methods
fields.note: auditpol disabling subcategories, stopping the EventLog service, or GPO/registry changes to auditing.

entries.summary: Turning off Windows auditing so subsequent actions go unlogged, often paired with, or preceding, log clearing.
entries.significance: A 4719 removing a sensitive subcategory, or a mid-session 1100, followed by an event gap is a strong evasion sequence.
triage: Alert on 4719 that disables Logon/Process/Object auditing.
Treat a 1100 without a reboot as suspicious.
Watch 4688 for auditpol /set /clear.
entries.caveats: GPO refreshes and hardening change audit policy legitimately, baseline expected changes.

entries.title: T1558.003: Kerberoasting

detection.telemetry: 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4); one account requesting many distinct SPNs quickly.

fields.name: Signature
fields.note: Bulk TGS requests (4769) for many service SPNs, RC4-encrypted, to crack service-account passwords offline.

entries.summary: Requesting RC4 service tickets for SPNs in bulk to crack service-account passwords offline.
entries.significance: Targets often-privileged service accounts with weak passwords. The 4769 distinct-SPN-per-account pattern is the detection.
triage: Hunt one account requesting many distinct ServiceNames (4769) in a short window.
Filter TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4).
Harden service accounts (long passwords, gMSA) and prefer AES.
entries.caveats: Legacy RC4 services create baseline noise, aggregate distinct SPNs per account.

entries.title: T1003: OS Credential Dumping

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 10 (LSASS access), Sysmon 11 (dump files), 4688 for dumping tools, 4662 for DCSync on DCs.

fields.name: Sub-techniques
fields.note: .001 LSASS Memory, .002 SAM, .003 NTDS, .006 DCSync, different sources, same goal of harvesting credentials.

entries.summary: Harvesting account credentials from LSASS, the SAM, NTDS.dit, or via DCSync, the gateway to escalation and lateral movement.
entries.significance: One of the highest-impact attacker actions. LSASS access (.001) is the most common on endpoints; DCSync (.006) targets domain controllers.
triage: Alert on non-security-tool access to lsass.exe (Sysmon 10) and .dmp creation (Sysmon 11).
Grep for comsvcs MiniDump, procdump -ma lsass, mimikatz, secretsdump.
On DCs, watch 4662 replication-rights use for DCSync.
entries.caveats: EDR/AV and backup tools touch these sources legitimately, allow-list known good.

entries.title: T1071: Application Layer Protocol (C2)

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 3 (connections), Sysmon 22 (DNS), and proxy/firewall logs for beacon cadence and rare destinations.

fields.name: Signals
fields.note: Regular-interval connections (beaconing), rare destinations, and interpreters/LOLBins initiating outbound traffic.

entries.summary: Blending command-and-control traffic into common application protocols (HTTP/S, DNS) to evade network defences.
entries.significance: The channel that keeps an intrusion alive. Process-attributed connections (Sysmon 3/22) turn 'some traffic' into 'this process is beaconing'.
triage: Attribute suspicious destinations to a process (Sysmon 3).
Hunt regular-interval connections (beaconing) to the same destination.
Flag LOLBins/interpreters making outbound connections.
entries.caveats: Legitimate apps beacon too (telemetry, updates). Baseline destinations per process.

entries.title: T1071.004: DNS (C2)

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 22 (process-attributed DNS) and DNS server logs; look for high-entropy/long subdomains and high query volume.

fields.name: Signals
fields.note: Long random-looking subdomains, unusual record types, and a single process resolving many odd domains.

entries.summary: Tunnelling command-and-control or data over DNS queries and responses.
entries.significance: DNS is rarely blocked and often under-inspected, making it a durable covert channel. Sysmon 22 attributes the queries to a process.
triage: Flag high-entropy/long QueryNames (Sysmon 22).
Attribute odd DNS to a process; interpreters are suspicious.
Correlate query volume/cadence with beaconing.
entries.caveats: CDNs and some software use long DNS labels legitimately. Baseline before alerting.

entries.title: T1098: Account Manipulation

detection.telemetry: 4728/4732/4756 (group adds), 4722 (enable), 4738 (account changed), 4724 (password reset).

fields.name: Methods
fields.note: Add accounts to privileged groups, re-enable dormant accounts, reset passwords, or alter attributes to keep access.

entries.summary: Modifying accounts, group membership, state, credentials, to maintain or escalate access.
entries.significance: Adding a controlled account to Domain Admins is a top escalation/persistence move. Group-management events are the primary signal.
triage: Alert on additions to privileged groups (4728/4732/4756).
Correlate re-enabled dormant accounts (4722) with subsequent logons.
Attribute changes to an operator and a change record.
entries.caveats: Legitimate admin onboarding produces these, alert tightly on privileged groups.

entries.title: T1136: Create Account

detection.telemetry: 4720 (user created), often followed by 4728/4732 group adds; net user / New-LocalUser in 4688.

fields.name: Sub-techniques
fields.note: .001 Local Account, .002 Domain Account. On endpoints, local account creation is rare and high-signal.

entries.summary: Creating new local or domain accounts for persistent access, frequently followed by adding them to privileged groups.
entries.significance: A durable backdoor. The 4720 -> 4732 sequence (create then elevate) is a textbook persistence pattern.
triage: Treat any endpoint 4720 as noteworthy; confirm against provisioning.
Look for a fast follow-on privileged-group add.
Check for net user / New-LocalUser in command lines.
entries.caveats: Provisioning, MDM, and domain joins create accounts legitimately, baseline automation.

entries.title: PowerShell 4103: Module / pipeline logging

detection.telemetry: Enable Module Logging via GPO (Windows Components > Windows PowerShell). Logs pipeline execution details and bound parameters per cmdlet.

fields.name: Payload / CommandInvocation
fields.note: The cmdlet invoked and its bound parameters, showing what each pipeline stage actually did.

fields.name: ContextInfo
fields.note: Host, user, and command line context for the invocation.

entries.summary: Module logging records pipeline execution details (cmdlets and parameters). It complements 4104 script-block logging with per-invocation context.
entries.significance: Where 4104 shows the code, 4103 shows the runtime pipeline, useful for reconstructing what a script did parameter-by-parameter and for catching living-off-the-land cmdlet abuse.
triage: Enable alongside Script Block Logging (4104) for full PowerShell coverage.
Review bound parameters for suspicious cmdlets (Invoke-WebRequest, Invoke-Expression, Get-Credential).
Correlate with 4104 and 4688 for the launching context.
entries.caveats: Very high volume. Admin automation generates enormous 4103 traffic; prefer 4104 for hunting and use 4103 for deep-dive reconstruction.

entries.title: Sysmon 8: CreateRemoteThread

detection.telemetry: Requires Sysmon with CreateRemoteThread logging. Captures one process creating a thread in another.

fields.name: SourceImage / TargetImage
fields.note: The injector and the injected process. A non-debugger process creating threads in another is a classic injection tell.

fields.name: StartAddress / StartModule
fields.note: Where the remote thread begins; an address outside a mapped module (or in an unexpected DLL) suggests shellcode injection.

entries.summary: Records cross-process thread creation, the core primitive of code injection (T1055). Attackers inject into trusted processes to hide and to steal tokens.
entries.significance: Process injection lets malware run inside a legitimate process (explorer, svchost). SourceImage/TargetImage pairs that are not normal debuggers, plus start addresses outside mapped modules, are strong injection signals.
triage: Flag SourceImage processes injecting into unrelated TargetImages.
Inspect StartAddress/StartModule for regions outside a signed module.
Correlate with Sysmon 10 (process access) and 7 (image loaded) for the full injection chain.
entries.caveats: Some security tools, debuggers, and legitimate software use remote threads. Baseline expected injectors.

entries.title: Sysmon 7: Image (DLL) loaded

detection.telemetry: Requires Sysmon with image-load logging (noisy, usually scoped to specific paths/processes or unsigned modules).

fields.name: ImageLoaded / Signed / Signature
fields.note: The DLL loaded and whether it is signed. Unsigned DLLs loaded by trusted processes are the DLL-hijack/side-load signal.

fields.name: Image
fields.note: The process that loaded the module. A signed app loading an unsigned DLL from a user-writable path is suspicious.

entries.summary: Records DLLs and modules loaded by processes. Scoped well, it catches DLL search-order hijacking and side-loading (T1574.002).
entries.significance: Attackers drop a malicious DLL next to a signed executable so the trusted process loads it (side-loading). Unsigned modules from temp/user paths loaded by trusted binaries are the tell.
triage: Flag unsigned ImageLoaded modules loaded by signed, trusted processes.
Look for DLLs loaded from user-writable paths adjacent to a signed EXE.
Correlate with Sysmon 1 (the process) and 11 (the DLL being written).
entries.caveats: Extremely high volume, must be scoped (e.g. unsigned-only, or specific processes). Legitimate software loads many unsigned DLLs.

entries.title: Sysmon 15: File create stream hash (ADS / Mark-of-the-Web)

detection.telemetry: Requires Sysmon with FileCreateStreamHash. Fires when a file with an alternate data stream (e.g. Zone.Identifier) is created.

fields.name: TargetFilename / Contents
fields.note: The file and its NTFS stream. Zone.Identifier records the download source (Mark-of-the-Web).

fields.name: Hash
fields.note: Hash of the stream content, pivot to intel.

entries.summary: Captures files created with NTFS alternate data streams, including the Zone.Identifier stream that marks internet-downloaded files (Mark-of-the-Web).
entries.significance: T1564.004. Reveals downloaded payloads (via Zone.Identifier) and data hidden in alternate data streams. Absence of MOTW where expected can indicate deliberate stripping to bypass SmartScreen/macro blocks.
triage: Use Zone.Identifier streams to identify internet-downloaded executables and scripts.
Flag executables/scripts hidden inside non-standard alternate data streams.
Correlate download source with process execution (Sysmon 1).
entries.caveats: MOTW streams are normal on all downloaded files. The signal is content hidden in unusual streams, or stripped MOTW on files that should have it.

entries.title: Sysmon 17 / 18: Named pipe created / connected

detection.telemetry: Requires Sysmon with named-pipe logging. 17=pipe created, 18=pipe connected.

fields.name: PipeName
fields.note: The pipe name. Default C2 frameworks (e.g. Cobalt Strike) use recognisable pipe-name patterns; random/known-bad names are leads.

fields.name: Image
fields.note: The process owning the pipe, attributing a suspicious pipe to a process is the value.

entries.summary: Records named-pipe creation and connection. Named pipes are used for local inter-process C2 (SMB beacons) and privilege-escalation via impersonation.
entries.significance: Post-exploitation frameworks use named pipes for peer-to-peer C2 and token impersonation. Known bad pipe-name patterns and unexpected processes owning pipes are the detections.
triage: Match PipeName against known C2 default patterns and threat intel.
Attribute suspicious pipes to their owning process (Image).
Correlate with Sysmon 8 (injection) and lateral-movement logons.
entries.caveats: Named pipes are heavily used by legitimate Windows IPC. Baseline normal pipe names; alert on known-bad patterns and anomalies.

entries.title: 5140 / 5145: A network share object was accessed

detection.telemetry: Audit File Share (5140) and Audit Detailed File Share (5145). Not on by default, enable on servers/DCs to track share access.

fields.name: ShareName
fields.note: The share accessed. Access to admin shares (C$, ADMIN$, IPC$) from unusual sources is a lateral-movement/tool-staging signal.

fields.name: IpAddress / SubjectUserName
fields.note: Who accessed the share and from where.

fields.name: RelativeTargetName (5145)
fields.note: The specific file within the share, reveals tool drops and data access.

entries.summary: Records access to SMB shares. Paired with network logons (4624 type 3), it exposes lateral movement over admin shares and tool staging.
entries.significance: T1021.002. Access to ADMIN$/C$/IPC$ underpins PsExec-style execution and remote tool drops. 5145 adds the file-level detail to see exactly what was written or read.
triage: Flag admin-share (C$/ADMIN$/IPC$) access from non-admin or unexpected sources.
Correlate with 4624 type 3 and 7045 service installs for remote execution.
Use 5145 RelativeTargetName to spot staged tools and exfiltrated files.
entries.caveats: Backup, deployment, and management tools access shares constantly. Baseline before alerting; 5145 is high-volume.

entries.title: 4662: An operation was performed on a directory object (DCSync)

detection.telemetry: Audit Directory Service Access with a SACL on the domain object. Logged on DCs. Needed to detect DCSync.

fields.name: Properties (control access rights)
fields.note: DCSync shows the replication GUIDs: DS-Replication-Get-Changes (1131f6aa-...) and DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All (1131f6ad-...).

fields.name: SubjectUserName
fields.note: The account performing replication. Non-DC accounts requesting replication is the DCSync signal.

entries.summary: Records directory-object access on domain controllers. Filtered to the replication rights, it is the detection for DCSync, pulling password hashes by impersonating a DC.
entries.significance: T1003.006. DCSync lets an attacker with the right privileges extract any account's hash (including krbtgt) without touching LSASS on a DC. A non-DC account exercising replication rights is a critical alert.
triage: Alert on 4662 with the DS-Replication-Get-Changes(-All) control-access GUIDs.
Confirm the SubjectUserName is an actual domain controller; anything else is suspicious.
Correlate with the source host and preceding privilege escalation.
entries.caveats: Domain controllers legitimately replicate constantly, so the detection depends on excluding real DC accounts. Requires SACL configuration.

entries.title: AppInit_DLLs: inject-into-every-process persistence

detection.telemetry: Monitor with Sysmon 13 / Security 4657. Should normally be empty; LoadAppInit_DLLs is usually 0.

fields.name: AppInit_DLLs
fields.note: DLLs listed here are loaded into every process that links user32.dll, a broad injection persistence. Normally empty.

fields.name: LoadAppInit_DLLs
fields.note: Enable flag; should be 0. A value of 1 with a populated AppInit_DLLs is suspicious.

entries.summary: A legacy mechanism that loads listed DLLs into nearly every GUI process. Rarely used legitimately today, so a populated value is high-signal.
entries.significance: T1546.010. Broad, powerful persistence and injection. Secure Boot disables it, but on systems without it, a populated AppInit_DLLs with LoadAppInit_DLLs=1 is almost always malicious.
triage: Confirm AppInit_DLLs is empty and LoadAppInit_DLLs is 0.
Investigate any listed DLL: path, signature, reputation.
Check both native and Wow6432Node keys.
entries.caveats: A few legacy accessibility/AV products used it historically. On modern hardened systems it should be empty.

entries.title: COM hijacking: CLSID persistence

detection.telemetry: Monitor with Sysmon 13 / 4657. HKCU CLSID entries that shadow HKLM ones are the abuse pattern.

fields.name: InprocServer32 (Default)
fields.note: The DLL servicing a COM class. Adding an HKCU CLSID entry overrides the machine one, so the attacker DLL loads when that COM object is invoked.

fields.name: TreatAs / LocalServer32
fields.note: Alternate COM registration paths that can be hijacked similarly.

entries.summary: Hijacks a COM object's registration so attacker code loads whenever a legitimate application instantiates that object, stealthy, often user-level persistence.
entries.significance: T1546.015. HKCU entries take precedence over HKLM for the current user, so no admin is needed. Triggers on normal application/OS activity, making it low-and-slow persistence.
triage: Diff HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID against expected; HKCU entries shadowing HKLM CLSIDs are suspect.
Resolve the InprocServer32 DLL and check path/signature.
Autoruns surfaces many COM hijack points; hide Microsoft-signed and review the rest.
entries.caveats: Some legitimate software registers per-user COM objects. Focus on user-writable DLL paths and unsigned modules.

entries.title: LSA Security Packages / SSP: credential-theft persistence

detection.telemetry: Monitor with Sysmon 13 / 4657. Values should be the known Microsoft packages only; additions load into LSASS at boot.

fields.name: Security Packages
fields.note: SSP DLLs loaded into LSASS. A rogue SSP (e.g. mimilib) captures plaintext credentials as users authenticate.

entries.summary: A malicious Security Support Provider registered here is loaded into LSASS and can log every plaintext credential at authentication time, persistence plus credential theft.
entries.significance: T1547.005 / credential access. Because the SSP runs inside LSASS, it is stealthy and captures credentials continuously. Any non-standard package name is high-signal.
triage: Compare Security Packages to the known Microsoft defaults; investigate any extra entry.
Resolve added SSP DLLs: path, signature, reputation.
Correlate with LSASS module loads (Sysmon 7) and credential-dumping activity.
entries.caveats: Third-party authentication products occasionally add SSPs legitimately, verify against your known software.

entries.title: BITS jobs: download & persistence via Background Intelligent Transfer

detection.telemetry: BITS-Client/Operational log records job creation and transfers. bitsadmin/PowerShell BITS cmdlets also show in 4688/Sysmon 1.

fields.name: Job command / notify
fields.note: BITS jobs can run a command on completion (SetNotifyCmdLine), the persistence/execution primitive.

fields.name: Remote URL / local file
fields.note: The download source and destination; BITS is a trusted downloader used as a stealthy cradle.

entries.summary: BITS is a trusted Windows transfer service. Attackers use it to download payloads quietly and to persist via jobs that run a command on completion.
entries.significance: T1197. BITS traffic blends in (it is how Windows Update downloads), and jobs survive reboots. bitsadmin /SetNotifyCmdLine and long-lived jobs are the abuse signals.
triage: Enumerate active BITS jobs (bitsadmin /list /allusers, or Get-BitsTransfer).
Flag jobs with a notify command line or suspicious remote URLs.
Review the BITS-Client/Operational log for unexpected job creation.
Correlate with 4688/Sysmon 1 for bitsadmin/PowerShell BITS use.
entries.caveats: BITS is used constantly by Windows Update and legitimate software. Focus on notify-command jobs and unusual sources.

entries.title: $MFT / $UsnJrnl: filesystem timeline

detection.location: Volume root: $MFT and $Extend\$UsnJrnl (raw NTFS metadata files)
detection.telemetry: Collect via forensic imaging / KAPE. Parse $MFT with MFTECmd; $UsnJrnl records file create/rename/delete operations.

fields.name: $STANDARD_INFORMATION vs $FILE_NAME times
fields.note: Compare the two timestamp sets; a mismatch reveals timestomping (T1070.006).

fields.name: $UsnJrnl records
fields.note: A change journal of file operations (create/rename/delete), reconstructs activity even for deleted files.

entries.summary: The NTFS Master File Table and USN change journal are the backbone of filesystem forensics, timelining file creation, modification, renaming, and deletion.
entries.significance: Rebuilds what happened on disk and when, including deleted files. Comparing $SI and $FN timestamps exposes timestomping; the USN journal shows the sequence of file operations around an incident.
triage: Parse $MFT with MFTECmd and build a filesystem timeline around the incident window.
Compare $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME timestamps to detect timestomping.
Use $UsnJrnl to recover the create/rename/delete sequence, including for deleted files.
Corroborate with Prefetch/Amcache for execution.
entries.caveats: $UsnJrnl wraps (finite size), so older entries roll off. $MFT resident data only helps for small files. Interpret timestamps carefully.

entries.title: T1055: Process Injection

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 8 (CreateRemoteThread), 10 (process access), 7 (image loaded), 17/18 (named pipes); EDR memory telemetry.

fields.name: Sub-techniques
fields.note: DLL injection, PE injection, process hollowing, APC/early-bird, and thread hijacking; all run code inside another process.

entries.summary: Running code inside another (usually trusted) process to evade defences, escalate, and access another process's memory.
entries.significance: A staple evasion technique; malware hides inside explorer/svchost and inherits trust. Cross-process thread creation and handle access are the primary signals.
triage: Alert on Sysmon 8 injections into unrelated processes and Sysmon 10 access to sensitive targets.
Look for start addresses outside mapped modules and unsigned injected DLLs (Sysmon 7).
Correlate with named-pipe C2 (Sysmon 17/18).
entries.caveats: Debuggers, AV/EDR, and some software legitimately inject. Baseline expected injectors.

entries.title: T1574: Hijack Execution Flow (DLL)

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 7 (unsigned DLL loaded by trusted process), 11 (DLL written next to an EXE), and service/path checks for unquoted paths.

fields.name: Common variants
fields.note: .001 DLL search-order hijacking, .002 DLL side-loading, plus unquoted service paths and phantom DLLs.

entries.summary: Placing a malicious library where a trusted program will load it (via search order, side-loading, or path interception) so attacker code runs with the host's trust.
entries.significance: Grants execution, persistence, and privilege by riding a signed binary. Unsigned DLLs loaded by trusted processes from user-writable paths are the tell.
triage: Flag unsigned DLLs loaded by signed processes (Sysmon 7), especially from temp/user paths.
Check services for unquoted paths with spaces and writable directories.
Correlate a DLL written (Sysmon 11) next to a signed EXE with its subsequent load.
entries.caveats: Legitimate software side-loads DLLs too. Focus on signature and path anomalies.

entries.title: T1564: Hide Artifacts

detection.telemetry: Sysmon 15 (ADS/stream hash), 11 (file create), 1 (hidden window / attrib), and MFT analysis for hidden/streamed data.

fields.name: Common forms
fields.note: NTFS alternate data streams, hidden files/attributes, stripped Mark-of-the-Web, and hidden windows/consoles.

entries.summary: Concealing files, data, and execution from users and defenders via alternate data streams, hidden attributes, or removing the Mark-of-the-Web.
entries.significance: Supports evasion across the kill chain. ADS-hidden payloads and stripped MOTW (to bypass SmartScreen/macro protections) are the common Windows forms.
triage: Hunt executables/scripts hidden in alternate data streams (Sysmon 15).
Flag stripped Mark-of-the-Web on files that should carry it.
Look for attrib +h / hidden-window launches in command lines.
entries.caveats: MOTW and some ADS use is normal. Focus on hidden executable content and evasive launch flags.

entries.title: T1197: BITS Jobs

detection.telemetry: BITS-Client/Operational log, 4688/Sysmon 1 for bitsadmin/PowerShell BITS cmdlets.

fields.name: Abuse
fields.note: Trusted downloader for payloads; jobs with SetNotifyCmdLine run a command on completion (execution/persistence).

entries.summary: Abusing the Background Intelligent Transfer Service to download payloads stealthily and to persist via completion-command jobs.
entries.significance: BITS traffic blends with Windows Update and survives reboots, making it a durable, low-profile channel.
triage: Enumerate BITS jobs (bitsadmin /list /allusers, Get-BitsTransfer).
Flag notify-command jobs and unusual remote URLs.
Review BITS-Client/Operational for unexpected jobs.
entries.caveats: Heavy legitimate use by Windows Update and software. Alert on notify commands and odd sources.

entries.title: T1558.001 / .002: Golden & Silver Tickets

detection.telemetry: Anomalous 4768/4769 (tickets with odd lifetimes, missing preceding 4768, or encryption/field anomalies); requires baseline knowledge of Kerberos flows.

fields.name: Golden vs Silver
fields.note: Golden forges a TGT using the krbtgt hash (domain-wide); Silver forges a service ticket using a service account hash (single service).

entries.summary: Forging Kerberos tickets from stolen key material: a Golden Ticket (krbtgt hash) grants domain-wide access; a Silver Ticket (service hash) grants access to one service.
entries.significance: Post-compromise persistence and lateral movement that can bypass normal authentication logging. A Silver Ticket may never generate a TGT request (4768), so a 4769/service use without a preceding 4768 is a lead.
triage: Baseline Kerberos flows; flag service-ticket use (4769) without a preceding TGT request (4768).
Alert on tickets with anomalous lifetimes or encryption downgrades.
Rotate krbtgt twice after suspected Golden Ticket use.
Restrict and monitor access to the krbtgt and service-account hashes.
entries.caveats: Forged tickets are designed to look legitimate, so detection is behavioural and imperfect. Protecting the underlying hashes is the primary defence.

entries.title: Events, alerts, cases and incidents
entries.summary: An event records an observation; an alert says logic found something worth review; a case organises analyst work; an incident is a confirmed or strongly suspected situation requiring coordinated response.
entries.significance: Confusing these objects produces bad decisions: a high-severity alert is not automatically a major incident, and several alerts may describe one incident. Preserve the source events and detection version so later case notes do not replace the evidence that triggered the work.
triage: Open the alert evidence and locate the original event rows.
Confirm rule version, time window, entities and collection health.
Test whether the observed behaviour occurred and whether it was expected.
Merge only records that share an evidence-backed activity or response scope.
Apply incident criteria using impact and confidence, not alert count alone.
Record closure or escalation reasoning, owner and next action.
entries.caveats: - Treating a vendor severity as business impact. - Counting duplicate alerts as additional affected systems. - Copying alert text into a case without preserving source evidence. - Declaring “no incident” when the real finding is “insufficient telemetry”.

Pivot to child processes, outbound connections, downloaded files and persistence changes.
Compare the script hash/path and identity with deployment tooling, administrator activity and change records.
Scope the same command fragments, hashes, URLs and accounts across telemetry before proposing containment.
entries.caveats: Do not run suspect content to “see what it does”, rely on process name alone, assume 4104 exists everywhere or treat every encoded command as malicious. `Get-WinEvent` timestamps and remote collection time zones must be normalised. A missing event may mean collection was disabled, overwritten or never configured, not that execution did not occur.

entries.title: Process Explorer
entries.summary: Process Explorer exposes process ancestry, owners, integrity levels, handles, loaded modules, signatures and live resource use so an analyst can test what a Windows process is and what it can reach.
entries.significance: Malware often runs through a trusted parent, loads an unexpected DLL or holds a handle to a sensitive process. Process Explorer helps you test those relationships on the host before you pivot to historical EDR, Event Log or Sysmon data.
triage: Locate the process in the tree and record its parent chain.
Open properties and capture image, command line, user, integrity and start time.
Verify the signature and inspect loaded DLLs or sensitive handles.
Compare the live state with EDR or event history for the same PID and time.
Document the evidence before requesting termination, isolation or collection.
entries.caveats: A valid signature proves who signed a file, not that the current behaviour is safe. Parent process IDs can be reused after a process exits. Run elevated only when the investigation requires protected details and your authority permits it.

examples.label: Read-only starting point
examples.code: Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Select-Object ProcessId, ParentProcessId, Name, ExecutablePath, CommandLine

entries.title: Process Monitor
entries.summary: Process Monitor captures file, Registry, process and thread operations with filters, call stacks and process context, letting an analyst reconstruct what a program attempted and what Windows returned.
entries.significance: Procmon can show the exact Registry value a process queried, the file it created, the DLL path Windows searched or the access result that changed execution. That detail bridges a high-level alert and the operating-system action behind it.
triage: Stop the default capture if you need time to define a narrow hypothesis.
Filter on the process, path or operation linked to the alert.
Reproduce only when authorised and record the exact capture window.
Inspect result codes, event properties and the process tree.
Export the filtered evidence and correlate durable changes centrally.
entries.caveats: Displayed filters do not reduce capture volume unless you configure drop filters. NAME NOT FOUND is common during normal search behaviour. A stack without matching symbols may not identify the responsible module.

examples.label: Read-only starting point
examples.code: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4657} -MaxEvents 50 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message

entries.title: PsExec
entries.summary: PsExec runs a process on another Windows system by authenticating over SMB, staging a service binary and asking the Service Control Manager to start it. Its value and its abuse potential produce a recognisable chain of network, logon, share, service and process evidence.
entries.significance: PsExec is legitimate administration and a common lateral-movement mechanism. The analyst's job is not to alert on the filename alone, but to reconstruct the complete remote-execution story: source host, initiating identity, target, authentication method, administrative-share access, service creation, launched command and follow-on behaviour. That chain also distinguishes real PsExec from tools that imitate its service-based technique while using another filename or service name.
triage: Anchor the target-side service or child-process event in UTC. Record service name, image path, account and command line.
Identify the source using 4624 source address, SMB/network telemetry and EDR remote-session context.
Build the target process tree from `services.exe` through the service binary to its children.
Review the initiating account's preceding authentication, privilege use and activity on other hosts.
Search for the same service image hash, pipe, account, source and command across the environment.
Ask the system owner for the change or support record. Compare source, target set, time and command, not just whether the team owns PsExec.
Preserve volatile process/network evidence before any approved containment, and document which links in the chain are inferred because telemetry is absent.
entries.caveats: - Treating 7045 as proof of PsExec: software installers and administrators create services too, while PsExec-like tools may choose another service name. - Looking only on the target: the source host contains the initiating process, credential-use and target list. - Assuming cleanup means no execution: the temporary service can disappear while retained logs still prove the chain. - Ignoring execution context: `-s`, alternate credentials and session options materially change impact and telemetry. - Running PsExec to test a theory: it creates the same evidence under investigation. Reproduce only in an isolated lab with approval.

entries.title: PsTools for defensive administration
entries.summary: PsTools provides command-line process, service, session, log and system-information views across local or remote Windows hosts, with PsExec forming the higher-risk remote execution member of the suite.
entries.significance: The suite can collect a consistent snapshot when PowerShell remoting or an EDR console is unavailable. The same remote features can expose credentials, create lateral-movement artefacts or change state, so analysts must choose the narrowest tool and record its effects.
triage: Define the information needed and select the read-only utility.
Confirm the source, target and approved response identity.
Record the command and expected network or authentication artefacts.
Preserve output and compare it with central telemetry.
Use PsExec or state-changing members only through response approval.
entries.caveats: PsLoggedOn can trigger remote Registry access and may not represent active interactive use. Remote results depend on firewall, service and privilege configuration. Administrative collection can resemble attacker discovery.

entries.title: RAMMap and VMMap
entries.summary: RAMMap explains physical-memory use across Windows while VMMap breaks one process into committed, private, mapped, image, heap and stack regions for focused memory triage.
entries.significance: Unusual private executable memory, unexplained mapped files or a process whose memory shape conflicts with its role can support an injection or unpacking hypothesis. These tools guide collection; they do not replace forensic acquisition.
triage: Decide whether the question concerns system memory or one process.
Capture process identity and the host timeline.
Review region type, protection and backing file.
Correlate unusual regions with threads, modules and process access.
Escalate to forensic acquisition before volatile evidence disappears.
entries.caveats: Memory protections change during normal runtime compilation. PID reuse and process exit invalidate live references. A map alone cannot prove the content or origin of a region.

examples.label: Read-only starting point
examples.code: Get-Process | Sort-Object WorkingSet64 -Descending | Select-Object -First 20 Name, Id, WorkingSet64, PrivateMemorySize64

entries.title: Sigcheck and signature trust
entries.summary: Sigcheck reports hashes, version metadata, entropy, signatures and certificate chains so an analyst can test a Windows file's identity without treating signing as a safety verdict.
entries.significance: Attackers rename binaries, copy signed tools and abuse vulnerable signed drivers. File path, hash, signer, certificate chain and observed behaviour together provide stronger identity than a filename or signature alone.
triage: Hash the file and record its full path and timestamps.
Inspect signature, chain and version metadata.
Compare the result with the approved software source and fleet prevalence.
Review process, network and persistence behaviour for the same hash.
Escalate conflicting identity or trust evidence without uploading the file by default.
entries.caveats: Signed malware and abused trusted tools exist. Revocation checks depend on network access and current trust stores. A high entropy value can reflect compression or encryption in legitimate software.

examples.label: Read-only starting point
examples.code: sigcheck.exe -accepteula -a -h -i 'C:\Path\suspect.exe'

entries.title: Sysmon architecture, configuration and event model
keywords: Sysmon architecture, configuration and event model
entries.summary: Sysmon uses a protected service and driver to record selected process, network, file, Registry, image-load and other activity in the Windows event log according to an explicit configuration.
entries.significance: Sysmon can preserve hashes, parent process GUIDs, network connections, DNS queries, file creation, Registry changes, named pipes and process access that standard audit policy may miss. Analysts must read the configuration before treating missing events as missing activity.
triage: Confirm Sysmon is installed, running and forwarding events.
Export or identify the active XML configuration and version.
Check whether the event class and field combination should be collected.
Correlate ProcessGuid, hashes, paths and destinations across event classes.
Record collection gaps before drawing a conclusion from absence.
entries.caveats: Event IDs only have meaning with the schema version and configuration. Broad image-load or network rules can create high volume. Attackers may tamper with collection, so compare host and central evidence.

examples.label: Read-only starting point
examples.code:

Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' -MaxEvents 20

entries.title: TCPView
entries.summary: TCPView maps current TCP and UDP endpoints to owning Windows processes and services, giving an analyst a fast live view of local addresses, destinations and connection state.
entries.significance: A destination IP has little value until you know which process opened it. TCPView joins live socket state to the process identity so you can distinguish a browser, service, update agent or unknown binary using the connection.
triage: Disable name resolution when you need untouched endpoint values.
Record the process, PID and endpoint tuple.
Inspect the owning process path, signer, parent and service.
Correlate the time and destination with retained network telemetry.
Preserve evidence before requesting connection closure or isolation.
entries.caveats: PID reuse can misattribute a connection after a process exits. UDP has no established state. Resolved names may reflect shared hosting rather than the application owner.

examples.label: Read-only starting point
examples.code: Get-NetTCPConnection | Select-Object State, LocalAddress, LocalPort, RemoteAddress, RemotePort, OwningProcess

entries.title: The Sysinternals suite
entries.summary: Sysinternals is Microsoft's portable Windows troubleshooting toolkit. Analysts use its focused utilities to inspect processes, persistence, files, permissions, memory and network state without installing a single all-purpose agent.
entries.significance: Windows telemetry often tells you that a process or connection existed without showing the live relationship an analyst needs. Sysinternals can expose the parent process, token, loaded DLL, open file, listening socket, persistence entry or effective permission that makes the event understandable. The suite is also used by administrators and attackers. A Sysinternals filename is not a verdict. Establish who launched it, whether it came from an approved location, what switches were supplied and what it did next.
triage: Define the question before choosing a tool: execution, activity, persistence, connection, trust, permission or memory.
Record hostname, UTC time, signed tool version, source path and operator identity.
Capture the narrowest useful output; filter high-volume tools such as Process Monitor before collecting.
Correlate the observation with retained logs so the finding survives after the process exits or the host changes.
Test the administrative explanation against change records, owner, target scope and command line.
Preserve exports with the case and state the tool's blind spots. Escalate only after separating observation from interpretation.
entries.caveats: - Starting every tool as administrator hides whether elevation was actually required and increases risk. - Process Monitor can collect enormous traces; begin with a time, process or path filter and set an output limit. - VirusTotal options can disclose hashes to an external service. Follow organisational policy before enabling them. - Live state is volatile. Do not replace retained event, EDR or forensic evidence with a screenshot alone. - A Microsoft signature proves publisher and file integrity, not that the current use is authorised or benign.

entries.title: Windows Event Logs and audit policy
keywords: Windows Event Logs and audit policy
entries.summary: Windows channels store provider events in EVTX logs, while audit policy decides which security actions generate records. Analysts must verify channel state, policy, retention, forwarding and field meaning before relying on presence or absence.
entries.significance: Windows events can connect authentication, process creation, services, tasks, policy and directory changes, but coverage is conditional. A defensible conclusion records the event's generating system, audit setting, collection route, retention and any delay or loss between endpoint and SIEM.
triage: Define the behaviour and exact provider/channel/event/version required.
Inspect effective audit policy and channel enablement on the affected asset class.
Query the endpoint or preserved EVTX, retaining record ID and XML fields.
Compare raw records with forwarded/SIEM copies and parser output.
Measure the available time window, rollover and collection delay.
Correlate with EDR, identity or network evidence and state explicit gaps.
entries.caveats: - Event ID without provider and version is ambiguous. - Missing events may mean disabled policy, rollover, forwarding failure or parser loss. - SIEM `TimeGenerated` may represent ingestion rather than the endpoint event time. - Rendered message strings are harder to parse reliably than event XML fields.
